articles.title: Tuned by Experience: Auditory statistical regularities shape attentional prioritization across pitch and timbre
articles.authors: Jason A Davis; Douglas A Addleman; Kevin Ortego; Viola S. Störmer
articles.abstract: Listeners navigate complex acoustic environments by selectively attending to relevant sounds amid competing noise. This capacity is classically attributed to top-down goals and bottom-up salience, but recent work implicates a third influence: selection history, whereby incidental exposure to statistical regularities shapes attentional prioritization. We investigated how incidental experience of selecting specific acoustic features influences attentional prioritization across different levels of auditory processing. Participants listened to two concurrently presented sounds to detect a target that contained a brief temporal gap. Unbeknownst to the participants, during a learning phase, one sound was more likely to contain the target gap; in a subsequent testing phase all sounds were equally likely to be the target. Experiment 1 used pure tones of varying pitches, and Experiment 2 used instrument chords (piano, trumpet, guitar). Across both experiments, participants responded faster to high-probability targets during learning, indicating facilitated attentional selection based on the statistical regularities across different levels of acoustic representations. This response time advantage persisted robustly throughout the unbiased testing phase for Experiment 1, but less so for Experiment 2, suggesting that the persistence of experience-driven auditory attention may depend on the complexity of the learned feature. Overall, our findings parallel selection-history effects observed in vision, providing evidence that similar influences of incidental experience on attentional priors exist across sensory modalities.

articles.title: Tracking vocabulary development as children start school: assessing measurement invariance in multilingual classrooms
articles.authors: Sonali Nag; Athina Ntalli; Gideon Arulmani; Joshua Aaron McGrane
articles.abstract: Receptive vocabulary, what is understood when hearing a word, underpins reading comprehension and wider learning. Yet, few tests have been validated to function fairly over developmental time and across diverse linguistic experiences. This study examined the Picture Test for Receptive Vocabulary (TalkTogether – Hindi), a 50-item test for four-to-nine-year-olds in multilingual north India. Words in the language of school instruction and linked images were drawn picture- and story books. Over one academic year (2023–2024), 1,949 administrations were collected from children (47% girls) at three time points across 40 schools. The test showed good reliability (Cronbach’s α = .82; Rasch reliability = .78) and captured variation across the proficiency range. Item properties remained stable across time, licensing its use as a fair tracking tool. Between-group differential item functioning (DIF) effects—by sex, home language(s), and a novel index of ambient peer language exposure—were small to negligible. The findings demonstrate that a contextually-situated vocabulary test, validated through rigorous psychometric evaluation, can meet the standards required for fair tracking of oral skills in the language of instruction. The reported protocol to inform item revision and evaluate dimensions of measurement invariance—demographic, contextual and developmental—are likely transferable to other similarly multilingual settings.

articles.title: Five Platform Functions and the Frustration–Aggression Pathway: A Mechanism Model of Grievance Identity Formation among Young Men
articles.authors: Johan G.L. Verheyden
articles.abstract: Aggression research holds that aversive experience raises aggressive readiness, but whether aggression is enacted depends on appraisal, cue exposure, reinforcement, and inhibition. This theory article specifies how digital platforms may modulate that pathway for young men exposed to identity-relevant status threat. It disaggregates platform effects into five functions: a social comparison amplifier, an identity threat accelerator, a cue-saturated environment, a reinforcement architecture, and an aggression affordance system. Each maps onto a component of the General Aggression Model, cognitive neoassociationism, or I³ Theory, and each is paired with a discriminant prediction that would count against that function if it failed. The article defines grievance identity as a self-schema marked by central in-group injustice, chronically accessible hostile attributions, legitimised adversarial behaviour, and peer recognition for hostile performance, and distinguishes it from collective victimhood, identity fusion, and ideological commitment. A six-stage pathway links identity-relevant goal blockage to inhibition erosion. The article engages with contested evidence on algorithmic recommendation, the selection-versus-amplification identification problem, and the generalisation gap in precarious manhood research. It reports no data and sets out an empirical agenda and conditions for falsification.

articles.title: Global Collective Pessimism: People predict a dystopian future and attribute it to political leaders
articles.authors: Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ann-Cathrin Coenen; Jonas R. Kunst
articles.abstract: Personal optimism is widespread. This research provides cross-cultural evidence for collective pessimism. Across four pre-registered experiments in 40 countries (N = 52,508), people believed it is much more likely that a future dystopian society will materialize than a utopian society. Dystopian predictions were driven not by internal attribution, but by asymmetric external attribution: People believed political leaders in society can exert greater influence on dystopian than utopian world development, and high leader impact was correlationally and causally linked to higher scenario likelihood. Text-based analyses revealed that participants named a political leader nearly twice as often in dystopias than utopias, and such personalized dystopias were considered more likely. Dystopian predictions were stronger among left-leaning individuals and in rich democracies, yet generalized across ideologies and world regions.

articles.title: Norms for Gender-Inclusive Role Nouns in Italian: The GIRN-I Database
articles.authors: Claudia Mazzuca; Chiara De Livio; Marta Mirabella; Guido Giovanardi; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Finding linguistic alternatives that move beyond the gender binary is increasingly indispensable, especially in languages that enforce gendered categorisations through specific linguistic markers, such as Italian. Indeed, gender-diverse individuals face additional distress associated with perceived invisibility arising from the absence of adequate linguistic forms.  To date, substantial research has been devoted to identifying demographic and socio-political factors underlying preferences for gender-inclusive language. However, far less is known about the cognitive mechanisms that underlie these attitudes. Here, we provide the first Italian psycholinguistic database of role nouns (e.g., nurse, carpenter, teacher) encompassing both gendered (i.e., feminine and masculine) and gender-inclusive (i.e., asterisk and schwa) desinences. Remarkably, this is the first contribution explicitly assessing Italian participants’ dispositions towards gender-inclusive desinences. We asked participants to rate role nouns on nine semantic dimensions, including classic dimensions like familiarity and sensibility and less conventional ones like psychological distance and political relevance. Our findings suggest no clear preference for either of the two inclusive alternatives, both of which are perceived as less familiar and less pleasant than their corresponding gendered forms. We suggest that processing components related to linguistic fluency may also contribute to explaining observed preference patterns. Taken together, our findings underscore the importance of considering semantic and linguistic processing factors, alongside ideological and social variables, when investigating attitudes toward gender-inclusive language.

articles.title: Can LLMs Grow Like Children? A Developmental Analysis of Capability Trajectories in Language Model Training
articles.authors: Ran An; Tingting Chung; Klaus Libertus
articles.abstract: Within two years, an infant who can barely lift her head learns to sit, reach, and walk. Developmental science found that this growth is both continuous and phased: skills improve smoothly, yet the pace of improvement changes at identifiable ages, and the field built statistical tools to locate those changes. Language models also transform across training, and whether their capabilities grow smoothly or in jumps is actively debated. The present study argues that the developmental answer applies to artificial learners as well, and that the developmental tools can show it. We apply an analysis pipeline built for infant motor development to the training trajectories of 16 open-source language models, each tested at 27 points during training on five benchmarks. The results mirror the infant findings. Growth is continuous but organized into phases, and transitions cluster at a small set of shared points that are deployed differently across domains. Growth proceeds slowly, then rapidly, then slowly, and models differ reliably in developmental rate. Unlike infants, those rate differences are almost entirely explained by model size. The transitions also survive changes of measurement scale, and on a continuous measure they appear earlier and more sharply than on accuracy. The paper contributes a formal test for phase structure in capability growth, a construct mapping between infant development and language model development, and evidence that phase structure may be a shared property of learning systems.

articles.title: Political Ingroup and Outgroup Cues Condition How Large Language Models Refute Conspiracy Theories
articles.authors: Erin B. Fitz; Kyle L. Saunders
articles.abstract: Despite emerging literature on conspiracy theories (CTs) in human-AI interactions, whether large language models (LLMs) refute CTs and how political identities affect responses remains unclear. Drawing on AI system documentation, positive politeness theory, and motivated reasoning research, we hypothesize that LLMs refute most CTs but adapt responses to the political identities of the user and actor in the claim. In a preregistered study comprising 135,845 conversations, 57 CTs, 21 user-actor political identity condition combinations, and seven OpenAI LLMs, we find that 82% of responses refute the CT and 20% exhibit motivated responding, i.e., acknowledge the user's perspective and affirm their concern. While refutation is more likely for CTs implicating Democrats or Republicans, motivated responding typically accompanies refutation and is more likely when claims involve the user’s outgroup---for example, when a Republican user inquires about a CT involving Democrats, and the model refutes the claim. Although responses to CTs implicating Republicans vary more by user identity than CTs implicating Democrats, the former attenuates response differences between outgroup and ingroup claims. These findings raise broader questions about what it means for AI models to be capable and reliable if LLMs consistently refute conspiracy theories but do so in politically asymmetric ways.

articles.title: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI: A Theoretical Framework for Memory, Metacognition, and Consumer Decision-Making
articles.authors: Chen Chen; Kristy Hamilton; Jacob T. Fisher
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow. A seven-stage delegation continuum maps increasing levels of offloading, and a value-based cost-benefit framework identifies its antecedents and the moderators that shape how consumers weigh them. We propose three clusters of outcomes. First, offloading weakens memory for brands and product attributes while strengthening memory for AI-generated summaries. Second, it inflates metacognitive self-esteem and decision confidence, producing AI-induced overconfidence that reduces further information-seeking. Third, effects on decision quality depend on AI reliability: when AI is unreliable, verifying AI recommendations imposes cognitive and emotional costs but can restore impaired memory and recalibrate inflated confidence. Seven propositions and three long-term conjectures extend these effects to consumer autonomy, competence erosion, and brand loyalty. Together, the CogOffload framework positions advertising in the era of Gen-AI as operating within a distributed system of human and artificial cognition.

articles.title: Being Observed by a Tutor Enhances Foreign Speech Production Learning in Video-Mediated Training
articles.authors: Qin Li; Piia Astikainen; Xueqiao Li; Shun Liu
articles.abstract: Social presence, particularly awareness of being observed by a tutor, may enhance learners’ engagement and attention during foreign language practice, but its effects on learning and associated neural activity remain poorly understood. We investigated whether learners’ (n = 32) awareness of being observed by a tutor influences foreign speech learning in a short (11-min) video-mediated listen-and-repeat training for Mandarin words. In the online group, learners knew the tutor could see them, whereas in the offline group, they knew the tutor could neither see nor hear them. Tone production was assessed before, during, and after training, and tone identification before and after training. Electroencephalography and autonomic activity were recorded during training. Tone production accuracy improved from pre- to post-training in the online group only, whereas tone identification improved similarly in both groups. Posterior alpha power increased during training in the offline group but did not change significantly in the online group. Together, these findings suggest that awareness of being observed by a tutor may support foreign language speech production learning in video-mediated settings. The accompanying differences in posterior alpha activity further indicate that the social context of learning is associated with differences in neural activity during practice.

articles.title: Gender-Inclusive Voice and Communication Training: Supporting Nonbinary Clients
articles.authors: Maura Philippone; Thea Knowles; Becks von Duering
articles.abstract: Nonbinary clients may pursue gender-affirming voice training (GAVT) goals that extend beyond traditional masculinization and feminization goals. This clinical perspective discusses potential applications of existing clinical frameworks for nonbinary clients, with particular focus on meta-therapy and the Acoustic Assumptions (AA) as gender-inclusive approaches. These approaches support gender-inclusive, person-centered exploration of voice and communication characteristics while drawing on established principles of speech production. Although further research is needed to establish more gender-inclusive acoustic and perceptual outcome measures, clinicians can presently use customizable, person-centered approaches to support diverse GAVT goals and provide affirming care.

articles.title: Risks and Opportunities in Digital Media Interventions for Youth: A Scientometric Review
articles.authors: Olivia Andrews; Mathilde E. Brons; I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; H.M. Koning Ina; Sophie Mary; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract:
Youth must navigate both the opportunities and risks associated with digital media. This
scientometric review examined 120 empirical studies on digital media interventions for youth
and used the 4C framework (content, contact, conduct, and contract) to map their thematic focus.
Scientometric mapping techniques were applied to explore keyword co-occurrence patterns and
collaboration networks. Most interventions addressed either risks or opportunities separately
(58.3%), whereas 39.2% combined risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension. Only
2.5% integrated multiple 4C dimensions. Interventions predominantly focused on content and
conduct, with limited attention to contact and contract, including topics like social interactions,
privacy, digital rights, and commercialization. Collaboration patterns were fragmented, with
researchers working within thematic clusters rather than across them, despite drawing on a
shared conceptual foundation. These findings suggest that current interventions cover only part
of the 4C framework. Future research should encourage more integrated, cross-dimensional
interventions and stronger collaboration among researchers.

articles.title: From Individual Gains to Collective Losses? The Socially Corrosive Path of Generative AI
articles.authors: Markus Langer; Igor Grossmann
articles.abstract: AI tools including generative AI (genAI) and agentic AI promise individual productivity gains, and users experience them as a resource that makes them more capable. However, research documents a robust social evaluation penalty for individual genAI use: people who use genAI, or are suspected of doing so, are judged as less competent, less diligent, and less caring. We argue that these judgments, followed through to their behavioral consequences, outline a socially corrosive path of collective genAI use. Along this path, when people substitute human contact with genAI and devalue what colleagues produce, relational interdependence, metaknowledge, and resulting opportunities for scalable collective intelligence decline, whereas trust erodes through a cycle of concealment, suspicion, policing, and blame. Current technology design and productivity narratives amplify these dynamics. We caution against waiting for genAI use to normalize and propose countermeasures: designing genAI for collective functioning, resisting the productivity trap, and making the social norms of genAI use explicit.

articles.title: Effect of Disclaimers on the Public Perception of AI-Generated Medical Advice: Two Preregistered Survey Experiments
articles.authors: Moritz Reis; Florian Reis; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used by the public as a source of medical advice, yet they can produce plausible but incorrect output. Disclaimers about the limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) are the most common safeguard and are also anchored in regulatory frameworks such as the European Union's AI Act. Whether disclaimers change how laypeople perceive and act on AI-generated medical advice, however, is unknown. We conducted two preregistered, randomized between-subjects survey experiments with US participants recruited via Prolific (study 1: N = 399; study 2: N = 396). Participants read four simulated dialogues in which a patient received medical advice from an AI tool and were randomized to see a disclaimer below the advice or no disclaimer. Study 1 used the standard disclaimer of a popular chatbot; study 2 used a stronger disclaimer that explicitly highlighted the higher risk of error compared with physicians and required participants to confirm having read it. Participants rated the advice’s empathy, reliability, and comprehensibility and their willingness to follow it. In study 1, the disclaimer did not significantly affect any outcome (all p > .17). In study 2, it did not significantly affect empathy, reliability, or comprehensibility (all p > .19). Willingness to follow the advice was slightly lower with the disclaimer (p = .039), but this effect did not remain significant after correcting for multiple testing. Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the two disclaimers. Disclaimers may thus serve mainly as transparency and liability measures and should not be relied on alone to protect users. Alternatives, such as communicating uncertainty within the response and strengthening AI literacy, deserve evaluation.

articles.title: How to Design a Panel Study for Investigating Bivariate Dynamics Using Continuous-Time Modeling
articles.authors: Nuria Real-Brioso; Eduardo Estrada
articles.abstract: Designing effective longitudinal panel studies to capture bivariate dynamics requires making informed decisions about how many measurements to collect and when to collect them. This study examines how design choices, concretely sample size, number of repeated measures, and various aspects of the temporal sampling schedule, influence the recovery of bivariate dynamic parameters in panel data analyzed using a Continuous-Time Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (CT-RI-CLPM). Through a Monte Carlo simulation, we tested a range of generating population parameters. We proposed a novel approach for planning sampling schedules: the Short-and-Long Lags design (SHALL) which deliberately mixes closely spaced and widely spaced intervals that continuous time models can accommodate. SHALL schedules are simple to understand and implement, and consistently ranked among the best sampling schedules in many scenarios. Our findings suggest that the number of repeated measurements and sample size significantly impact parameter recovery, particularly for cross-lagged effects, which exhibited low estimation efficiency even in the most favorable conditions, leading to low statistical power. We provide actionable recommendations for researchers planning panel data studies, along with open-source R code to facilitate the design of SHALL sampling schedules. We also provide R code to implement a CT-RI-CLPM to new data sets. An empirical example illustrates the application of such a model to data from an empirical panel study relating self-esteem and depression. This work contributes evidence-based guidance for improving the design and analysis of longitudinal panel studies using continuous-time modeling.

articles.title: Getting ready for minority language transmission: Language management preparation among expecting parents in Fryslân
articles.authors: Suzanne Victoria Dekker; Jelske Dijkstra; Pavlina Heinzova; Mirjam Vellinga; Ruth Kircher
articles.abstract: This study examines a previously unexplored aspect of family language policies: namely how expecting parents prepare for language management, focusing on their engagement with language-related resources – books, leaflets, magazines, etc. – to support them in getting ready to raise their children (bi-/multilingually) with a minority language. We collected questionnaire data from 520 participants in the province of Fryslân, the Netherlands. The majority language of the Netherlands is Dutch; Fryslân is home to most speakers of the minority language Frisian. Quantitative data were analysed statistically, qualitative data were analysed using conventional qualitative content analysis. Findings show that most participants decided what language(s) to transmit prior to pregnancy. Furthermore,  expecting parents who ultimately ended up transmitting Frisian were more aware of, and used more, resources than parents who ultimately did not transmit Frisian. The former also indicated a desire for additional resources to support bilingual (Dutch-Frisian) child-rearing and Frisian transmission. The paper discusses the study’s implications for policy and planning aiming to promote the intergenerational transmission of Frisian, and thereby promoting its maintenance and revitalisation.

articles.title: A Three-Wave RI-CLPM Linking Adolescent Affect and their Engagement with Sustainable Development
articles.authors: Richard Anthony Inman; Sara Ribeiro de Faria; Paulo Moreira
articles.abstract: This study examines reciprocal relationships between affect and engagement and disengagement with sustainable development in a cohort of 580 Portuguese adolescents assessed serendipitously before COVID-19 (ages 12-13), during lockdown (ages 13-14), and approximately one year after lockdown (ages 13-14). Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modelling (RI-CLPM) distinguished stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. Adolescents with higher negative affect generally reported lower engagement and higher disengagement. Within individuals, higher-than-usual negative affect before the pandemic predicted greater subsequent disengagement during lockdown. In turn, higher-than-usual negative affect during lockdown predicted greater subsequent engagement. No cross-lagged effects involving positive affect or from engagement or disengagement to affect were statistically significant. The findings suggest that negative affect may precede different responses to sustainable development across contextual conditions. Efforts to promote engagement should therefore consider adolescents’ emotional experiences alongside their circumstances, rather than assume that negative affect necessarily undermines engagement or that evoking it will encourage sustainable action.

articles.title: Development Insights and User Experience of a Preventive Digital Parenting Intervention for Adolescent Mental Health
articles.authors: Rick van Logchem; Crystal R. Smit; Anne Bülow; Hanneke Scholten; Bart Soenens; Loes Keijsers
articles.abstract:
Background: Despite being hailed as a promising avenue for preventing increasingly prevalent adolescent mental health problems, digital parenting interventions to strengthen adolescent mental well-being remain scarce. How such interventions are developed and experienced by end-users provides key insights for their later implementation and contextualizes information on their effectiveness, yet little systemic evidence is available.
Objective: To inform optimal development and aid careful evaluation of digital parenting interventions, this preregistered multimethod study served three aims. First, to identify theoretical, functional, and user-derived lessons for digital parenting interventions for adolescent mental well-being, distilled from the challenges of developing a novel digital parenting intervention. Second, to examine user experience in terms of feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness as early markers of implementation success. Third, to understand whether user experience is linked to characteristics of the intervention (i.e., universal versus personalized delivery), parents (e.g., openness to advice), or adolescents (e.g., depressive symptoms).
Methods: Development of the intervention was based on Self-Determination Theory and followed an iterative process, including focus groups with parents and adolescents, a pilot study among n = 12 families and subsequent exit-interviews, and a brainstorm session with experts (n = 6). The intervention was evaluated among parents (N = 199, Mage = 47.6, SDage = 4.7), resulting in administrative and daily diary data of user experience (feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness). Baseline data were used to test whether intervention, parent, and adolescent characteristics related to user experience.
Results: Findings suggest that adolescent perspectives align with the tenets of self-determination theory as a framework that can be translated to concrete advice for parents, that the frequency and delivery of advice should fit family routines, and parental agency and choice were important user needs. Feasibility, adoption, acceptability, and appropriateness were sufficient according to our preregistered criteria, but there was substantial heterogeneity between parents and within parents (across days). User experience did not differ between a personalized and universal version of the intervention. Parents who were generally more open to advice, and parents of boys, younger adolescents, and less depressed adolescents evaluated the intervention more favorably. 
Conclusions: Findings suggest that the fit between our intervention and parents differed substantially across parents, and from tip tot tip, highlighting the need for further refinement of our digital parenting interventions before implementation, and the consideration of user experience throughout development.

articles.title: An Individual-Level Paradigm for Research on Deception Cues: An Urgent Proposal
articles.authors: Erik Mac Giolla; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: All psychological theories of deception cues concern explanatory mechanisms at the level of the individual. However, past research on deception cues compares the behavior of people telling the truth and lying at the group level. Unless two conditions are met, that the statistical models do not vary (i) across individuals or (ii) across occasions in time, group-level findings cannot accurately describe the behavior of individuals. We show that these conditions are unlikely to hold for deception cues. This means the current group-level research cannot provide a meaningful test of the individual-level mechanisms key to understanding deception cues. In order to draw meaningful conclusions about these individual-level mechanisms, the field needs a wholly different research paradigm, based on repeated measures designs. We outline a proposal for such an individual-level research agenda and argue that without this development, fundamental questions in deception research will remain unanswered and theories of deception will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Statistical distinguishability of psychopathology symptom network and common factor models in longitudinal data
articles.authors: Sakari Johannes Lintula; Jaakko Tammilehto; Suoma Saarni; Tom Rosenström
articles.abstract: Psychometric conceptualizations of psychopathology have gained popularity. Most prominent approaches are the common factor (CF) and the symptom network models. A known problem in theory development through empirical findings is the statistical indistinguishability of CF and symptom network models in cross-sectional data. However, the extent of this problem and its implications have not been inspected formally for longitudinal studies. In this study, we sought to clarify the distinguishability between CF and symptom network models in longitudinal designs. We show necessary and sufficient conditions for indistinguishability in covariance for commonly applied vector autoregressive symptom network models and CF models and suggest a procedure for assessing whether a CF model can be refuted based on an estimated symptom network model. We give easy-to-implement R -functions for conducting the comparison. Numerical and empirical examples show that potential indistinguishability is relevant when interpreting the published literature. Overall, this study promotes comparative analysis of symptom network and CF models.

articles.title: Familiar words iconicity shapes novel words meaning
articles.authors: Daniele Gatti; Celia Martínez Tomás; José Antonio Hinojosa
articles.abstract: Iconicity, the perceived resemblance between a word’s form and meaning, is systematically related to the semantic organization of familiar vocabulary. This raises the possibility that iconicity-related regularities also constrain how people interpret unfamiliar words. We tested this proposal by learning mappings from (sub)lexical representations to large-scale English iconicity ratings and examining whether predicted iconicity for pseudowords was associated with the semantic quality and specificity of human-generated definitions. Higher iconicity predicted from semantic representations was associated with definitions that aligned more closely with their target pseudowords and distinguished them more selectively from alternative forms. In contrast, orthographic features predicted iconicity in familiar words but showed no corresponding associations with pseudoword definitions. The positive associations for semantic representations generalized across multiple encoders, including analyses in which different models were used to predict iconicity and evaluate definitions. These findings suggest that iconicity-related semantic structure in familiar vocabulary is associated with the construction of meanings for unfamiliar forms. They are consistent with discriminative and complementary learning accounts in which previously acquired form-meaning relations provide graded constraints on novel interpretations and, more broadly, they connect theories of iconicity grounded in perceptual and experiential resemblance with distributional accounts of lexical knowledge, suggesting that linguistic experience organizes and supports the generalization of resemblance-related semantic information to novel forms.

articles.title: Gambling Marketing in Young Adults’ Digital Media Environments: Exposure, Gambling Risk, and Momentary Responses
articles.authors: Priska Breves; Lauranna Teunissen; Eva van Reijmersdal; Merel Walraven; Martin-Pieter Jansen; Hilde Voorveld
articles.abstract: Advertising restrictions largely remove gambling marketing from mass media, but digital channels, from social media to e-mail, leave room for paid, owned, and earned messages that are difficult to monitor. In a seven-day ecological momentary assessment, 178 Dutch online gamblers aged 18–30 documented encounters with gambling marketing with a screenshot or photo; all 1,377 images were content-analysed. At least one encounter was reported in 42% of assessment intervals and high-risk gamblers recalled more marketing encounters than other participants. Half of the documented marketing came from Instagram or Facebook, half offered a financial inducement, and one in fourteen messages came from unlicensed operators or impersonated licensed brands; high-risk gamblers mostly documented operators’ own posts, the other groups mostly paid ads. At encounters, participants reported a stronger urge to gamble, anticipated more positive outcomes and more escalation of their gambling, and expected to feel less guilty about gambling than in their own unexposed moments. Additionally, gambling was more likely in the same interval as an encounter. Gambling marketing thus remains a routine part of young gamblers’ digital media use and encounters coincide with momentary shifts towards gambling.

articles.title: A Multimodal Study of Screen Use in Adolescents Across Brain Structure, Social Media, and Gaming Use
articles.authors: Wesley Lo; Richard B. Lopez; Benjamin Nephew
articles.abstract: In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population. Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret. For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use. This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends. Whether these patterns are reflected in the brain also remains largely unexplored. ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) is well suited to these questions because of its comprehensive profiling across neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical domains. In a preregistered study, we examined how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity. All five confirmatory associations were positive but small (β = 0.051 to 0.173) and remained consistent across several robustness checks. In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were. The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants. More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ. In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly. Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself. Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study. We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

articles.title: Risk in Context: How Weather Influences Consumer Responses to Climate Risk
articles.authors: Zeynep Aslan; Antonia Krefeld-Schwalb; Bram Van den Bergh
articles.abstract:
Protecting homes from increasing climate hazards depends in part on consumers’ understanding
and acting on objective climate risk information. Yet such information is not interpreted in
isolation. Interpretation may be influenced by immediate contextual cues. This research examines
how weather conditions, as one example of relevant contextual cues, influence consumers’
responses to property-level climate risk information. Pairing website visit data from an online
platform providing flood risk information with the weather data at users’ location, we demonstrate
that weather is associated with interest in personal climate-hazard risk. Specifically, visits to the
website increase following periods of rainfall and decline during extended dry spells at the users’
locations. Beyond generating interest in climate-hazard risks, we show in four experiments that
weather moderates the effect of objective climate-hazard risk on consumers’ judgments. When
weather conditions contradict the objective risk, consumers’ judgments shift away from the direction
implied by the objective risk information. In contrast, when weather aligns with the objective
risk, weather effects are mostly absent. These effects also trickle down to consumers’ willingness
to adopt protective measures. These findings advance our understanding of consumers’ evaluation
of risks by showing that heterogeneity in risk perception and protection motivation can emerge
from an asymmetric integration of objective risk information and immediate contextual cues depending
on whether the signals align or not.

articles.title: Conspiratorial mentality among older people: The role of loneliness, depression, anxiety, and social media use
articles.authors: Michal Mužík; Jan Serek
articles.abstract: Despite age being a significant sociodemographic correlate of conspiratorial mentality, surprisingly little is known about its precursors and consequences among older people. Older people are often considered at risk of psychological distress, which often relates to conspiratorial mentality. Our study therefore assumed bidirectional relations between these constructs. Distress was represented by loneliness, anxiety, and depression. We also investigated potential moderation by social media use, as conspiracy theories tend to be disseminated on such media. We tested these associations linearly and quadratically using data from a two-wave longitudinal study of Czech adults aged 60+ (NW1 = 4133, MageW1 = 69.1). Conspiratorial mentality was not predicted by other variables, indicating that these are probably not risk factors for such mentality. Conversely, conspiratorial mentality positively predicted only anxiety. Social media use moderation and quadratic effects were unsupported. Overall, the study suggests that conspiratorial mentality can be an anxiety-provoking experience among older people.

articles.title: Chronic Pain as a Complex Dynamic System: Conceptual Foundations and a Narrative Review of Network Approaches
articles.authors: Saskia Scholten; Gwen van der Wijk; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Felicitas Kininger; Julia Glombiewski; Johan W.S. Vlaeyen
articles.abstract:
Despite extensive medical, psychological, and social research and substantial healthcare investment, chronic pain remains highly prevalent, and a leading cause of years lived with disability. While multimodal and interdisciplinary treatments are recommended, progress may be limited by the lack of an integrative theoretical framework that captures the complexity of chronic pain across levels of analysis.
We introduce a complex dynamic systems perspective as a unifying theoretical framework in which chronic pain emerges from interactions among biological, psychological, and social components over time, and we present a methodological toolbox based on the network approach to operationalize this perspective by modeling such interactions.
We conducted the first narrative review of network studies in chronic pain, identifying 54 studies published up to June 30, 2026. Most studies used cross-sectional network models to examine associations among pain-related variables, comorbidity patterns, and group differences, whereas longitudinal and within-person approaches were rare. Across studies, findings support the view that chronic pain-related factors form interconnected systems; however, substantial heterogeneity in variable selection and study design limits comparability and generalizability.
Overall, current applications provide an important first step toward modeling the complexity of chronic pain but so far remain limited in capturing temporal dynamics and individual-level processes. Advancing this field will require theory-driven, multi-level, and longitudinal research that aligns network methods with system-level questions. In the longer term, this approach holds the promise to support the development of parsimonious models of key mechanisms, informing interventions that target not only symptoms but the dynamic processes that sustain chronic pain.

articles.title: Relational Mobility and the Sharing of Positive and Negative Reputation Across Societies
articles.authors: Haruno Kusakabe; Masaki Yuki
articles.abstract: The sharing and use of reputational information about others are fundamental to human societies. Yet little is known about how the sharing of positive and negative reputational information varies across socio-ecological conditions. We examined its associations with relational mobility, a socio-ecological factor pertaining to the freedom and opportunity to form and select interpersonal relationships. Across three surveys in the United States and Japan (total N = 930), participants reported perceived prevalence of positive and negative reputational information in their local social environments. In Study 2, they also reported their own everyday sharing. For positive information, US participants reported a higher perceived prevalence and more self-reported sharing than Japanese participants, and within-country associations with relational mobility generally supported our predictions. For negative information, within-country associations were generally negative, as predicted, but country differences were either nonsignificant or opposite to the predicted direction. Indirect effects via perceived relational mobility were consistent with our predictions for both positive and negative information across studies. These findings highlight the importance of considering both socio-ecological context and reputational valence in research on reputation.

articles.title: Differing Conceptions of Interpersonal and Intergroup Conflict Resolution Across the Lifespan
articles.authors: Jacob Glassman; Katherine McAuliffe
articles.abstract:
Conflicts between individuals and between groups are common across human relationships, making effective conflict resolution essential for flourishing societies. Yet, how conceptions of interpersonal and intergroup conflicts develop with age remains largely unexplored. We investigated perceptions of, expectations about, and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts in children (N = 97, Mage = 7.54, 45% female, 41% White), adolescents (N = 180, Mage = 13.17, 43% female, 59% White), and adults (N = 201, Mage = 38.98, 54% female, 78% White) tested in 2023. Participants viewed transgressions with ambiguous perpetrator intent between an individual perpetrator and an individual victim (interpersonal) or between a group perpetrator and a group victim (intergroup). All participants perceived more negative intent and expected less forgiveness in intergroup conflicts than in interpersonal conflicts, while adolescents and adults also punished more, and adults additionally expected less trust and perceived greater transgression severity. Harsher perceptions and expectations in intergroup relative to interpersonal conflicts were explained by greater intentionality being attributed to group perpetrators than individual perpetrators. With age, children increasingly perceived more negative intent and expected less trust in intergroup conflicts, appearing increasingly adultlike. Findings demonstrate that, compared with interpersonal conflicts, harsher conceptions of intergroup conflicts emerge early in development and strengthen across the lifespan.

Keywords: Conflict, conflict resolution, intergroup, interpersonal, social cognitive development

articles.title: The Third Allostasis: a biophysical displacement of regulatory purpose in neurodivergent, high-ability and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh)
articles.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira; Pricilla Braga Laskosky
articles.abstract: Patients within the neurodivergent spectrum, high-ability profiles, and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh) frequently present a clinical paradox: marked cognitive domains alongside debilitating functional collapse, burnout, dysautonomia, and migrating multisystem symptoms. Standard cross-sectional laboratory investigations against population references routinely prove inconclusive or trigger fragmented, iatrogenic interventions. Here, we define the Third Allostasis: an evolutionarily conserved biophysical regime wherein the organism displaces peripheral homeostasis and lowers systemic throughput to defend central nervous system membrane viability when environmental and informational demands approach the kinetic limits of transmembrane ion clearance. Through within-person longitudinal follow-up of five adult HPCPh trajectories—spanning stepped recovery from decade-long containment, live entry into acute biological helplessness, endothelial–natriuretic decompression, cognitive restoration, and exit from chronic matrix dysautonomia—we demonstrate how this regime becomes clinically visible using four routine laboratory instruments. We introduce accessible arithmetic tools for any consulting room: the red-cell hydration index (Ht-3×Hb) and two "Rules of Three" (OsmP@290 and Na@290) that unmask hidden plasma osmolal gaps driven by uncharged organic osmolytes, even when raw osmolality and sodium remain within normal limits. Crucially, while an open osmolal gap signals fast-axis intercompartmental shift, clinical direction requires "whole-column reading" across slower coupled buffers, including circadian cortisol, tissue thyroid gating (FT3/rT3), iron-ferritin dynamics, prolactin, and monocytes. Recognizing the Third Allostasis shifts clinical practice from treating isolated organ abnormalities to reading the organism's adaptive effort as a whole, guiding contextual adjustments that relieve central overload and restore functional vitality.

articles.title: How Does Profile Text Signal Desirability in Online Dating? A Meta-Analysis of Cue Valence and Explicitness
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Signaling mate desirability is central to a well-functioning online dating market. This meta-analysis examines how profile text signals the owner's desirability. Drawing on research on negativity and cue diagnosticity, warranting theory, and signaling theory, I test how the valence (positive vs. negative) and explicitness (explicit vs. implicit) of text-based cues shape viewers' reactions. I analyzed 13 experiments (53 effect sizes) drawn from a scoping review of online dating research. Text-based cues have a small, heterogeneous effect on evaluations, dating intentions, and behavior toward the profile owner (g = 0.25). Negative cues move responses (g = 0.38), whereas positive cues do not (g = −0.07). Explicit and implicit cues do not differ overall, but the gap between negative and positive cues is larger for explicit cues. The results show that strategic verbal content in online dating profiles works as a screening device, carrying meaningful information about undesirable traits in a partner.

articles.title: Changing moral beliefs and behaviors using human-AI dialogues
articles.authors: Joshua Paul White; Carter Allen; Lucius Caviola; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Moral beliefs are widely considered resistant to change, yet the rise of conversational AI offers new tools for moral persuasion. We report a preregistered experiment (N = 500) in which participants were randomly assigned to a 5-round conversation with an AI agent prompted to persuade them that either eating meat, or not giving to charity, is morally wrong. Conversations produced large and immediate shifts in moral beliefs in the intended direction (Cohen’s d = 0.37–0.48), along with corresponding behavioral effects: participants in the charity conversation condition donated 16.35% more of their bonus money to charity than participants in the meat conversation condition, while those in the meat conversation condition were 25.04 percentage points more likely to choose a plant-based over a beef burger voucher compared to those in the charity conversation condition. One month later, the effect on burger voucher choice remained significant, while other effects did not. NLP analysis of participant moral justifications and AI persuasive strategies suggests that moral persuasion was partly driven by factual correction—particularly in the meat domain, where factual appeals to the naturalness and biological necessity of meat eating were the most common among participants—alongside direct moral argumentation. These results demonstrate that human-AI dialogues can produce meaningful change in moral beliefs and behavior, raising important questions about the capacity of conversational AI to shape human values at scale.

articles.title: Registered Replication Report and Extension of Maas & Hox (2005), Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models
articles.authors: Joao F Guassi Moreira; Jared Block; Alondra M. Cruz; Craig K. Enders; Amanda Kay Montoya
articles.abstract: The use of multilevel models in behavioral and social sciences has risen dramatically in the past several decades. Researchers using these models often consult highly-referenced simulation studies when designing their own studies, especially for sample-size planning.However, current literature suggests two issues with this practice. First, recent efforts to replicate findings from seminal simulation studies suggest the rate of replicability is far from ideal (Luijken et al., 2024). Second, researchers are now using more complex models but foundational simulation studies were conducted under much simpler conditions. To address these two issues, we propose a replication and extension of Maas & Hox (2005), a widely cited study that recommended Level-2 sample sizes of N = 50 to be sufficient under specific conditions. We replicate their core findings and propose several extensions based on a literature search of multilevel modeling practices employed in fifty recent studies.These extensions include examining conditions with imbalanced data across higher-level units, varying the number of random slopes and cross-level interactions, and varying effect sizes. These results could ensure the existing literature relies on a replicable simulation study while also informing multilevel study planning for complex models which are becoming increasingly popular in behavioral and social sciences.

articles_hidden.title: The Feasibility of Conducting Research on Cannabis Use in Early Adolescents in England
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Huang; Leah Fawaz; Amanda Sarpong; Shareha Saiady; Chloe Dagcevizi; Solveig Carer; Kelly Charge; Maria Livanou; Jake Camp; Amy Lineham
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Approximately 10% of early adolescents in the UK report lifetime cannabis use. However, contemporary UK research in this population remains limited due to recruitment, consent and safeguarding challenges. We explored the feasibility of conducting research about cannabis use in UK adolescents aged 13–15 years.

Methods: This exploratory feasibility project comprised an online quantitative survey and qualitative interviews on cannabis use and mental health. Participants aged 13-15 years were recruited through schools, drug services, social media, posters and word-of-mouth. Participants consented through either a standard parent-and-adolescent pathway or an independent Gillick-competent pathway. Feasibility outcomes included total recruitment, cannabis-user recruitment, successful data collection, and the extent of safeguarding actions required. 

Results: 175 participants completed the survey (Mage = 14.35, 54.9% female) and n=13 (7.4%) reported lifetime cannabis use. 16 participants (Mage=14.56, 75.0% female) completed the qualitative interview study, including 11 lifetime cannabis users. Two and four cannabis-using participants used the Gillick-competent pathway in the quantitative and qualitative studies, respectively. In the quantitative study, 38/175 participants (21.7%) triggered low-intensity signposting and one participant received additional safeguarding actions. Three qualitative participants received safeguarding actions. Both studies successfully elicited detailed information on cannabis use, mental health and contextual experiences.

Conclusion: We recruited nearly 200 13-15-year-old adolescent participants, including those who used cannabis, collected rich data about illegal cannabis use and mental health using in-depth surveys and interviews, while keeping participants safe. We therefore proved we can feasibly conduct research about cannabis in <16-year-olds in the UK.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking the Integration of Novel Words into the Mental Lexicon: Evidence from Mouse Movement Trajectories
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew P. Lucas; Richard J. O'Connor; Kevin J. Riggs; Shane Lindsay
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated lexical competition effects in novel word learning using mouse tracking methodology. We conducted two experiments examining how and when novel word representations become lexicalised, focusing on their ability to engage in competition with existing lexical entries. In Experiment 1, we used mouse tracking to conceptually replicate Weighall et al.’s (2017) eye tracking study, examining lexical competition between newly learnt word–referent pairs and familiar words both immediately after learning and following overnight consolidation. Mixed-effects analyses demonstrated immediate lexical competition effects for novel words. Competition did not differ significantly between words learnt on the previous day and those learnt on the day of testing. Experiment 2 demonstrated that displaying the referent associated with a newly learnt phonological competitor increased immediate lexical competition, even when targets in both conditions had trained phonological neighbours. The temporal dynamics of mouse trajectories revealed that familiar words produced earlier and larger peak competition effects compared to newly learnt words. These findings support models of word learning that allow for rapid lexical integration, while acknowledging that newly formed lexical representations may not immediately exhibit the same processing characteristics as well‑established words.

articles_hidden.title: Capacity Limits in Cognitive Processing Reflect the Curse of Generalization
articles_hidden.authors: Steven M Frankland; Raja Marjieh; Marco Nurisso; Joseph Fluegemann; Taylor Webb; Giovanni Petri; Richard L. Lewis; Jonathan D. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract:
The striking constraints of some human cognitive processes stand in stark contrast
to the near limitless capability of others. While we can acquire and flexibly use vast amounts
of information, the amount we can process at any one time is often stiflingly limited: for
example the number of items we can hold in working memory or the number of tasks that can
be performed at once. Here, we integrate ideas from information theory, cognitive science,
and neuroscience to offer a unified account of why processing is often so limited. We argue
that this reflects a fundamental tradeoff between generalization—how effectively existing
representations can be used in novel settings—and how many distinct representations can
be processed in parallel. Representations that best promote strong forms of generalization
— a characteristically human cognitive strength — come at the expense of surprisingly
strict limits in the number of items that can be processed at once, an equally characteristic
human weakness. We refer to this as the “curse of generalization.” We formulate this first in
information-theoretic terms, and then in process models, including a neural network model
of classic tasks used to demonstrate strict limits in human processing capacity. This tension
offers a potential explanation for a range of phenomena — from performance on the tasks on
which we focus, to representational learning and skill acquisition more broadly — as well
as the performance of modern machine learning architectures that exhibit generalization
capabilities comparable to humans.

articles_hidden.title: Value-based control over memory encoding and search
articles_hidden.authors: Sven Wientjes; Clay B. Holroyd; Sean Matthew Polyn
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory is an adaptive cognitive function that enables individuals to use past experiences to guide future behavior. Prior research has demonstrated that goal-relevant, or rewarded, items are remembered more effectively, but the underlying mechanisms—ranging from automatic neuromodulation to strategic elaboration—remain debated. In this study, we investigated how different reward structures influence the temporal organization of free recall in mixed-item lists. Rewards were administered either during item encoding or were contingent on successful later recall. Our behavioral results reveal a striking mid-list primacy effect: when rewards are contingent on later recall, participants disproportionately initiate search at the onset of rewarded subsequences, effectively treating reward shifts as privileged access points. To account for these findings, we developed a novel hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the context maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of free recall. By fitting the model to individual recall sequences, we adjudicated between competing accounts of memory enhancement. Our results demonstrate that motivated memory relies on two key mechanisms: the strengthening of context-to-item associations and the strategic creation of accessible event boundaries. These findings suggest the primacy effect involves the strategic reinstatement of a privileged context rather than solely the enhanced encoding of early list items. With regard to executive control and event segmentation theories, this suggests that participants exercise fine-grained control over their mental context, perhaps through varying mnemonic techniques. We propose that motivated memory is not merely a product of enhanced associative binding, but also involves active, structured (re)organization of experience.

articles_hidden.title: Shared and distinct patterns of cortical network-level functional connectivity associated with child psychopathology dimensions
articles_hidden.authors: Lei Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Improving current understanding of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying child mental disorders could inform the development of effective therapeutic interventions. The United States National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) advocates to study neural correlates of child psychopathology using dimensional approach. Using baseline data from 8,970 children aged 9-10 years (50.37% male) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, I applied bifactor modeling to decompose Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) into one general psychopathology factor and three specific symptom factors (Conduct Problems, ADHD, Internalizing Problems) and studied the association of both shared and specific factors with cortical network-level functional connectivity using multivariate method aiming to delineate both shared and distinct patterns of functional organization associated with different child psychopathology. The result showed that increased general psychopathology was associated increase bottom-up processing of sensorimotor hand and auditory information and top-down processing of visual information; increased Conduct Problems showed increased cognitive neglect of visual and sensorimotor information and elevated sensorimotor and auditory network activities; increased ADHD showed sustained abnormality in both top-down and bottom-up processing of motor and auditory information; increased Internalizing Problems showed hyperactivities in cognitive control, top-down and bottom-up processing, visual information processing and hypoactivities in bottom-up processing of visual information and spatial navigation as well as maintaining spatial navigation. Sensitivity analysis including race yielded largely consistent result. Adjusting for socioeconomic status attenuated the associations with Conduct Problems and Internalizing Problems, whereas associations with General Psychopathology and ADHD remained robust. My findings offered novel insights into neurobiological mechanisms of different child psychopathology and suggested altered functional organization of the brain could serve as a potential biomarker for child mental disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Bioengineering an improved niche for neural stem cells
articles_hidden.authors: Yash Parikh
articles_hidden.abstract: Aging is one of the key drivers of cognitive decline and slowing neurogenesis. It is a major risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases. In the process of aging, neural stem cells stop proliferating at a high level, and the niche surrounding them begins to undergo extensive change. This large shift consists of vascular changes, lower growth factor signaling, higher stiffness and tension, and reduced cell-to-cell interactions. In research to date, in vitro models have not recreated a full neural stem cell niche while taking into account all of the previously listed factors. In this proposal, a bioengineered, 3D niche specifically designed to recreate the environment of a young neurogenic niche is constructed. The niche will have the stiffness of its hydrogel extracellular matrix tuned, growth factors added and co-culturing of glial cells with neural stem cells. The neural stem cells, from aged mice and from young mice, will be sowed into the target niche and two controls, which will be developed into organoid systems. Measurements of two neuronal proteins in these organoids will demonstrate how successful the bioengineered niche will be at restoring neurogenesis to aged neural stem cells. This work could show how much of age-related cognitive decline is driven by the surrounding niche rather than intrinsic issues with the cells. Additionally, a successful organoid would also be exceptionally useful for disease modeling and for modeling strategies to restore neurogenesis in the aging brain.

articles_hidden.title: Does CBT change the brain? A systematic review of neuroimaging RCTs on anxiety disorders, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Ioulia Kokka; Iraklis Mourikis
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety disorders, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but the neurobiological mechanisms of change remain unclear. This systematic review synthesized neuroimaging evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether CBT can be considered a neurobiological intervention. Following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251239465), PubMed, Scopus and PsycInfo were searched for RCTs of CBT in adults with anxiety disorders, depression or OCD-spectrum disorders reporting pre- and post-treatment neuroimaging. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, and findings were synthesized narratively. Seventeen RCTs were included (OCD = 5, anxiety disorders = 6, depression = 6), using task-based fMRI (n = 8), resting-state fMRI (n = 6), structural MRI (n = 2) or PET (n = 1). Changes after CBT involved emotional reactivity regions, prefrontal and frontoparietal control systems and their connectivity, with disorder-specific patterns: reduced threat reactivity in anxiety disorders, altered cognitive control networks in OCD, and altered mood-related, self-referential and reward connectivity in depression. Neural and clinical change did not always coincide, and comparisons with pharmacotherapy were mixed. Five studies were at high risk of bias. These findings provide preliminary support for CBT as a neurobiological intervention, although small samples and heterogeneous protocols limit conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Conditions as Processes: Developmental Features and Clinical Implications
articles_hidden.authors: Vadim Pérez Koldenkova
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental disorders are typically approached as syndrome-defined states, and questions like why conditions outlast their triggers, why diagnoses overlap, why some resist treatment, how change occurs and what recovery should aim at are usually addressed separately. Here, we approach mental health conditions as processes within a person’s lifelong development, putting forward four propositions: 1) maintenance and development compete for a limited capacity for change; 2) repeated activity becomes structure; 3) self-maintenance can turn into entrapment, which depletes finite reserves; 4) reorganization is often abrupt and lasts only if consolidated. From this perspective, mental health appears as the preserved capacity to keep developing, whereas many persistent conditions appear as active entrapment—a pattern reproduced by the person’s own activity (avoidance, rumination). Therefore, entering a state, remaining in it, leaving it and stabilizing the outcome can depend on different conditions. For each of these phases we derive clinical implications and testable predictions.

articles_hidden.title: The Morality of Partiality: How Relationship Expectations Shape Moral Evaluations
articles_hidden.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Amiya Shelly Aggarwal; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Alexander C. Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations. The present research (N = 3,417) examined how people evaluate partial and impartial actors who prioritized either a socially connected other (family member, friend, or community member) or a stranger in need. Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors. This preference was strongest when impartial actors failed to prioritize a close (family member or friend), rather than more distant (community member), social tie. Impartial actors were also perceived as less predictable and as fulfilling less of their relational obligations, with these perceptions predicting judgments of their moral character. In Experiment 4, participants themselves exhibited a preference for partiality, with most preferring to help a socially connected other over a stranger in greater need. This preference was stronger when decisions were described as publicly observable rather than anonymous, consistent with reputational concerns influencing helping decisions. Together, these findings suggest that everyday moral judgments reflect not only assessments of adherence to abstract ethical principles but also inferences about individuals’ reliability as long-term social partners.

articles_hidden.title: Imagery Instructions Reduce False Memories Across the Visual Imagery Spectrum
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaonan Li; Wilma A. Bainbridge
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual mental imagery is widely theorized to support memory by enhancing the richness and distinctiveness of encoded representations. However, it remains unclear how imagery ability interacts with different encoding strategies to shape memory performance. The present study examined how encoding modality (imagery vs. verbal) and processing focus (item-specific vs. relational) interact with visual imagery ability to influence veridical and false memory in the Deese–Roediger–McDermott (DRM) paradigm. A total of 173 participants (71 aphantasic participants, 12 intermediate, and 90 typical imagers) completed ten DRM lists under one of four encoding conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects design. Our results suggest that true recall did not differ reliably between different encoding strategies, nor was it consistently predicted by Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) scores, indicating that imagery ability does not broadly determine veridical memory accuracy. In contrast, imagery-based encoding reduced false memories (critical lure recall) compared with verbal encoding across the range of imagery abilities. Notably, individuals with aphantasia, despite reporting greater difficulty implementing imagery instructions, showed comparable benefits from imagery-based encoding. This finding suggests that the mnemonic benefits of imagery-based strategies may not depend exclusively on conscious visual imagery and may involve alternative representational processes. These findings challenge the assumption that imagery vividness predicts memory performance and open new avenues for understanding compensatory encoding mechanisms in aphantasia.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond accuracy: extracting reaction-time biomarkers of sustained attention and cognitive flexibility from the UCancellation task
articles_hidden.authors: Boris Penaloza; Elnaz Vafaei; Jaap Munneke; Anja Pahor; Susanne M. Jaeggi; Aaron R. Seitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories. Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework. RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index. Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load—large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased—consistent with inhibition of return. Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric Refinement of the Cognitive Assessment in Music Therapy for Institutionalized Older Adults (ACPIM-5)
articles_hidden.authors: Mariana Lacerda Arruda; Frederico Gonçalves Pedrosa; Gislaine Cristina Vagetti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: This study psychometrically refined the Cognitive Assessment of Older Adults in Music Therapy (ACPIM) and evaluated its convergent validity and longitudinal stability relative to the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). 
Method: Participants included 180 institutionalized older adults (mean age = 79.0 ± 8.2 years; 93.9% cognitively impaired). Psychometric refinement integrated Network Psychometrics, Rasch Partial Credit Modeling, and Confirmatory Factor Analysis. 
Results: MoCA items required category collapsing to resolve disordered thresholds. Refinement yielded a unidimensional 5-item scale (ACPIM-5) demonstrating adequate fit (χ²(4) = 4.039, p = 0.401; CFI = 1.000; TLI = 1.000; RMSEA = 0.007, 90% CI [0.000, 0.113]; ω = 0.896) and high fidelity with the 18-item version (r = 0.930). A bifactor model confirmed to be a dominant General Factor (H = 0.896; factor determinacy = 0.928) convergent with the MoCA (r = 0.380). ROC analysis demonstrated acceptable preliminary discrimination (AUC = 0.768, 95% CI [0.593, 0.943]; cutoff = 12.5; sensitivity = 72.8%; specificity = 81.8%).
Discussion: The ACPIM-5 satisfied 7-day metric invariance (Δχ²(5) = 3.418, p = 0.636), confirming factor loading equivalence. In contrast, the MoCA violated scalar invariance (Δχ²(20) = 43.896, p = 0.0015), indicating threshold drift. The ACPIM-5 provides a context grounded, rapid screening metric for music therapy with institutionalized older adults.

articles_hidden.title: A Multilevel Signal Detection Theory Approach to Unconscious Processing Research
articles_hidden.authors: Ricardo Rey-Sáez; Alicia Franco-Martínez; Miguel A. Vadillo; Francisco Garre-Frutos
articles_hidden.abstract: To test for unconscious processing, researchers typically compare measures of a stimulus’s influence on behavior with measures of awareness of that stimulus. Three common hypotheses are often tested: whether influence is significant while awareness is not (group-level dissociation), whether both measures are independent across participants (correlation), or whether influence persists when awareness is extrapolated to be zero (regression intercept). Conventional analyses suffer from three well-known methodological limitations: First, both measures often differ in scale and number of trials, complicating meaningful comparisons of their relative sensitivities. Second, analyses based on participant-level sensitivities ignore measurement error, which attenuates correlations and inflates regression intercepts, leading to misleading evidence for unconscious processing. Third, the correlation hypothesis requires evidence of null association, but conventional significance tests provide limited evidence for the absence of an effect. To address these problems, we introduce a multilevel signal detection theory (SDT) model that jointly analyzes trial-level responses from both measures and allows all three hypotheses to be tested directly while accounting for measurement error. The model supports both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, allowing researchers to run non-superiority tests and quantify evidence for null hypotheses using Bayes factors. We illustrate this approach through reanalyses of three published studies on unconscious processing. The {uSDT} R package provides an accessible way to fit the joint multilevel SDT model and evaluate all three hypotheses more rigorously.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Expectancies and Interpretations: A Transdiagnostic Mediation Model of Intolerance of Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Elinor Abado; Julie Lin Ji; Julian Basanovic; Colin MacLeod; Anne Schacht; Marcella Lydia Woud
articles_hidden.abstract: Expectancy and interpretation biases are widely considered transdiagnostic markers of psychopathology, yet the nature of their relationship remains understudied. If these processes are causally related, modifying one may influence the other and reduce associated symptoms. Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is a transdiagnostic trait linked to biased interpretations and their modification. The present study tested a mediation model in which interpretations were hypothesized to mediate the relationship between expectancies and IU. According to this account, expectancy-related ratings were expected to predict interpretation-related ratings, which in turn were expected to predict trait IU. In an online study, N = 263 unselected participants completed a novel task in which each trial paired an expectancy sentence and rating with a subsequent interpretation sentence and rating, jointly assessing both processes. Sentence valence (neutral/emotional) and expectancy-interpretation outcome pairings (e.g., positive-positive, positive-negative) varied randomly across trials. Results showed that more negative expectancy and interpretation ratings were associated with higher levels of trait IU, anxiety, and depression, whereas more positive ratings were associated with lower levels of each. In a cross-sectional mediation model, expectancies showed significant direct paths to both interpretations and IU, but interpretations did not mediate the expectancy-IU relationship. These findings point to a central transdiagnostic role for expectancies relative to interpretations. Interventions may therefore benefit from prioritizing expectancy biases; nonetheless, the observation that expectancy and interpretation biases were associated with symptom measures in opposing and complementary directions indicates that joint assessment of both cognitive processes remains more informative than assessing either alone.

articles_hidden.title: Auditory Working Memory Is Susceptible to Intrusions from Subsequent Sounds
articles_hidden.authors: Manda Fischer; Keisuke Fukuda
articles_hidden.abstract: As sounds unfold over time, listeners often need to relate successive events while keeping them distinct. Auditory working memory is susceptible to interference from subsequent sounds, yet whether resulting errors reflect distortion of the remembered target or intrusion of the intervening sound itself remains unclear. Although both mechanisms can produce similar average biases toward an intervening sound, they predict distinct distributions of reproduction errors. Recent advances in continuous pitch reproduction now allow us to test these predictions in audition. In two experiments, participants remembered a target tone over a brief delay and reproduced its pitch on a circular continuous-response scale. During the delay, an intervening tone was presented; participants either ignored it or judged its similarity to the target. We analyzed reproduction-error distributions with mixture modeling to distinguish systematic shifts in target-centred responses (i.e., distortion) from responses clustered around the intervening pitch (i.e., intrusion).  The results showed that the error distributions were better accounted for by models incorporating responses centred near the intervening pitch (i.e., intrusion) than the models assuming continuous displacement of target-centred responses alone (i.e., distortion). Exploratory analyses suggested that the influence of task relevance of the intervening sound was associated with baseline memory precision: listeners with less precise baseline reproduction tended to show greater interference when told to explicitly compare the sounds. Together, these findings suggest that intervening sounds may do more than bias reports of remembered pitch.
