On some trials, the intervening sound may guide the final response in place of the target, even when task-irrelevant.

articles_hidden.title: Uncertainty Weighting as a Time-Invariant Principle of Crossmodal Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Manda Fischer; Keisuke Fukuda
articles_hidden.abstract: In a dynamic world, events unfold and disappear, often providing only fleeting or incomplete sensory evidence. Information from another sense may help us interpret these encounters, but what determines how strongly it influences what we later remember? Across two audiovisual working-memory experiments, we tested whether auditory context exerts greater influence when visual information is reconstructed less reliably. Participants viewed a face morphed along a feminine–masculine continuum for 100ms and, after a 1,900-ms retention interval, reproduced it using a continuous face-morph response wheel. On cue trials, a feminine- or masculine-sounding voice was presented 1,000ms before face onset (prediction) or 900ms after face offset (postdiction). In Experiment 1 (N=84), voice cues shifted reconstructions toward the cued gender in both tasks. Across observers, weaker visual sensitivity was associated with greater auditory influence; and within observers, faces reconstructed less consistently without cues showed stronger bias. Experiment 2 (N=170) extended this relationship to externally imposed visual uncertainty through resolution reduction and spatial occlusion. Across both manipulations and cue timings, less reliable reconstruction was associated with greater auditory cue influence. Despite this consistency in uncertainty-sensitive auditory influence, the way voices influenced reconstructions depended on whether they were heard before or after the face. Together, these findings suggest a recurring functional principle of crossmodal inference: The less reliably visual information can be reconstructed, the more strongly contextual information influences the resulting judgment. Differences in how auditory bias was expressed suggest prediction and postdiction may address the same inferential challenge through different underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: Phronesis (Practical Wisdom) as a Measure of Moral Excellence:  A Comparative Study of Business and Non-Business Students at a Joint-Venture University in China
articles_hidden.authors: Yan Huo; Hyemin Han; Shane McLoughlin; Eddy Fang; Kristján Kristjánsson
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study compares mastery of phronesis (i.e., practical wisdom) between business school students and students in other schools at a joint-venture university in China. We inquired whether business students’ practical wisdom was more evident or less evident compared with the non-business students. Our question was motivated by the existing research in the business ethics literature that does not provide a ‘happy reading’ about business students, whose qualities are often associated with dishonesty, greed, corruption, and selfishness, more so than those of non-business students. We utilised the Short Phronesis Measure (SPM), which was recently developed and validated; it assesses moral functioning holistically, different from most conventional measures that focus only on individual traits or virtue/vice constructs. We collected data from 653 participants (business students, n=289; non-business students, n=364). Our Bayesian analysis of the data showed that business students’ phronesis mastery was not significantly different from that of non-business students in all domains. The finding suggests that business students are not inferior in phronetic moral functioning in general. This serves as an important reminder for business school educators that business students have the same potential as other students to achieve moral excellence.

articles_hidden.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles_hidden.title: From Formal Theory to Personalized Treatment: A Precision Mental Health Roadmap
articles_hidden.authors: Nathaniel R Choukas; Sharina Hamm; Donald Robinaugh; Dawson Haddox; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Eiko I Fried; Denny Borsboom; Shirley B Wang; Zachary Daniel Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence-based psychotherapies benefit many patients, but individual outcomes vary and guidance for personalizing treatment remains limited. The verbal theories underlying these treatments describe processes thought to produce improvement but often leave their strength, direction, functional form, and timescales unspecified. This limits theory-informed predictions about how a particular patient would respond to alternative treatments. Researchers have begun formalizing theories of psychopathology in mathematical or computational form to address these limitations. Formal theories make theoretical assumptions explicit, allowing precise and testable predictions to be deduced analytically or through computational models. When these models represent treatment effects and relevant individual differences, researchers can use patient measurements to inform model states and parameters, simulate alternative treatment configurations, and compare predicted outcomes. Empirical evaluation must distinguish the accuracy of outcome predictions, support for the proposed mechanisms, and whether model-guided selection or adaptation improves outcomes relative to other treatment selection strategies. Translating this potential into practice requires aligning the theory with patient assessment, treatment delivery, and evaluation. We propose a roadmap for this process and describe conditions supporting the generation, delivery, and testing of formal theory-driven treatment recommendations. A worked example using a formal theory of panic disorder and a modular digital therapy illustrates the roadmap’s early phases, including provisional model extensions that generate different treatment predictions for two simulated patients. We conclude by discussing challenges in theory development, patient matching, measurement, and empirical evaluation that must be addressed before these predictions can guide clinical care.

articles_hidden.title: Validity and Age Sensitivity of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality: A Comparison with the Paper-and-Pencil Test in Younger and Older Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Dante O’Connor; Sarah E. MacPherson
articles_hidden.abstract: The Trail Making Test (TMT) is among the most widely used neuropsychological tests, and its completion times slow with age. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR) preserves the sequencing structure of the test but replaces pen movements with head-gaze selection in an immersive environment. However, the convergent validity and sensitivity to age of its English-language version in older adults are unknown. Forty-seven younger (20–38 years) and 44 older adults (64–81 years) completed the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR in counterbalanced order. Nine scores were derived per format from Parts A and B: completion times, errors, error-adjusted times, and B−A difference scores. Part A and Part B completion times and error-adjusted times of the two formats correlated significantly in the whole sample, and Part B completion times did so within each age group, whereas errors did not. Older adults performed more poorly than younger adults on completion times in both formats, and the age groups were thus differentiated by both the paper-and-pencil TMT and the TMT-VR. The TMT-VR differentiated the age groups statistically better than the paper-and-pencil TMT on Part B completion times, error-adjusted times and errors, but both formats performed comparably on Part A scores. No paper-and-pencil score distinguished between the groups better than its TMT-VR counterpart. The TMT-VR is therefore a valid immersive adaptation of the TMT, and its advantage in age sensitivity lies in the Part B scores. Future studies should aim for clinical validation in older adults.

articles_hidden.title: The longitudinal relation between motor and language skills at two and four-to 4.5 years of age in a large Singaporean cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Havron; Hugo Peyre; Yap Seng Chong; Birit F.P. Broekman; Lourdes Mary Daniel; Shirong Cai; Sho Tsuji
articles_hidden.abstract: Early language is intricately related to the development of other skills. Motor skills, in particular, have been associated with language development, but the precise relations between these domains is a matter of ongoing research. Here we examined the longitudinal relations between fine- and gross-motor skills and language abilities in a large population cohort (N = 885, 49% female) from Singapore. Using a cross-lagged panel model with data from 9 to 48 months of age, we investigated both within-time associations and directional effects between motor and language domains. We found significant concurrent associations between motor and language skills. Fine-motor skills at 9 months predicted language development at 18 months, even after controlling for demographic factors. None of the other cross-domains paths was significant. In order to explain this discrepancy with past research, we therefore also explored without controlling for these factors. This latter  analysis revealed more predictive paths from gross and fin- motor to language development, from the age of 9 months up to two years, suggesting that previous findings might be explained by confounding factors. Our findings highlight the importance of controlling for confounding factors when examining the relation between motor and language development.

articles_hidden.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles_hidden.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles_hidden.title: The Developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP): Continuous Word Reading Difficulty Estimates of the 9,961 Most Frequently Printed English Words for US Children
articles_hidden.authors: Donald Compton; Jay Rueckl; Laura Steacy; Noam Siegelman; Ashley Edwards; Yaacov Petscher; Nicole Patton Terry; Matthew James Cooper Borkenhagen; Chelsea Starke
articles_hidden.abstract: The developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) is a database comprising word reading data for 9,961 of the most frequently printed English words for children, including continuous IRT-based estimates of word reading difficulty, accompanying word characteristics, and raw trial-level data. Data on isolated word reading accuracy were collected from 1,907 children in grades 1-5 across multiple US sites. Each child read a list of words ranging from 250 to 500 items depending on reading skill (less proficient children were often unable to finish the entire list of words), with each list representing the full distribution of word difficulties oversampled for words at the child’s reading level. Each child also attempted 99 linking items representing the full distribution of word difficulties. A total of 631,322 total responses were collected with the average child providing 336. For the final sample of words, the average number of responses per word for the 9,862 non-linking items was 47.14 (range of 10-592) and for the 99 linking items the average was 1681.42 (range of 1083-1907). A Rasch model, with planned missing design, was fit to children’s responses on the word list and linking item responses. This introduction describes the motivation for this project; the methods used for data collecting; the analytic framework used to establish a continuous measure of word reading difficulty across words; descriptive statistics of the relational database and initial behavioral results; and a publicly available search engine providing searchable access to the word difficulty ratings and associated word-level statistics.

articles_hidden.title: Behavioral dimensions and white matter organization in early childhood following preterm birth
articles_hidden.authors: Sakshi Kaur; David Vanier; Dennis Dimond; Kirk Graff; Ryann Tansey; Amanda Ip; Shelly Yin; Daria Merrikh; Christiane Rohr; Lily Koochak
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Children born preterm are at increased risk for attentional, social and emotional challenges, collectively referred to as the preterm behavioral phenotype. While white matter alterations have been linked to individual behavioral domains following preterm birth, it remains unclear whether distinct dimensions of behavioral variability are associated with specific patterns of white matter organization. Understanding neurobiological risk markers for preterm phenotypic traits may help identify children at greatest risk. 
Objective: We investigated the extent to which these behavioral traits covary across the gestational age spectrum and whether latent behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter micro- and macro-structure in young children born preterm. 
Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm (29 females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks). Principal component analyses were performed separately in preterm, full-term, and combined groups to characterize latent behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning. Fixel-based analysis was then used to examine associations between behavioral dimensions and fiber density and fiber cross-section, adjusting for demographic and perinatal factors.
Results: In the preterm sample, autism- and ADHD-related behaviors emerged as relatively distinct dimensions, whereas behavioral variance in the full-term sample was captured by a broad neurodevelopmental dimension. In children born preterm, higher scores on the ADHD-related behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section in the splenium of the corpus callosum. No significant associations were found for fiber density in the preterm or full-term samples. 
Conclusions: These findings suggest that prematurity influences not only behavioral outcomes, but also how those outcomes relate to white matter organization, highlighting the importance of considering behavioral heterogeneity when investigating brain-behavior relationships in preterm populations.

articles_hidden.title: Failure to distinguish “mental health” from “mental illness” disrupts effective policy for population well-being
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Ruggeri; Hannes Jarke; Sofia Pelica
articles_hidden.abstract: The semantics and measurement of “mental health”, “well-being”, and “mental illness” have long been debated - as has the way clinicians and policymakers are expected to respond to their associated insights. However, despite existing discussion on distinctions between these terms, there is an urgent need to more forcefully articulate how key terminology in mental health should be used. Failures to do so have been problematic and directly impacted how mental health is understood, which has subsequently impacted efforts to prevent and treat mental illness as well as protect and promote mental health. Here we highlight significant concerns about incorrect use of these terms, their implications, and why the field needs to urgently apply more stringency in the literature. Our aim is not to criticize journals, articles, or authors for such mixing, but rather to provide compelling arguments as to why it is critical to be correct and precise about how these are discussed, measured, and addressed to benefit population well-being.

articles_hidden.title: The Dark Triad and trait aggression in women and men: Clarifying the substantive consequences of factor overlap
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolás González-Raposo; Pablo Polo; Eduardo Galaz Villarroel; Katrin Schaefer; Bernhard Fink; Todd K. Shackelford; Virgil Zeigler-Hill; Tobias Koch; Ulrich S. Tran; Jose Antonio Muñoz Reyes
articles_hidden.abstract: Although the Dark Triad (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) has been consistently linked to aggressive behaviors such as bullying and violence, two important questions about these associations remain unresolved. First, little is known about how they differ between women and men. Second, it remains unclear how factor overlap affects their substantive interpretation. Drawing on evolutionary accounts of intrasexual competition, we predict stronger associations with physical and verbal aggression in men and hostility in women. We test these predictions on Short Dark Triad and Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire data from 600 Chilean adults, using bifactor (S−1) structural equation modeling. We find that Machiavellianism predicts all aggression outcomes, psychopathy-specific variance positively predicts physical aggression, and narcissism-specific variance negatively predicts hostility. Sex differences in aggression overlap with sex differences in aversive traits, but none of the Dark Triad-aggression associations consistently differ by sex. By introducing the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE), we provide the first substantive translation of these bifactor associations. VWLE clarifies how reference facet and trait-specific associations reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism, making the implications of residual coefficients explicit.

articles_hidden.title: Menstrual Cycle Status and the Acute Subjective Psychedelic Experience
articles_hidden.authors: Alaina Srivastav; Sunjuri Sun; Peter Hendricks; Walter Osika; Cecilia Ulrika Dagsdotter Stenfors; Sankalp Chaturvedi; Michelle Olofsson; Gabriella Smedfors; Simon Goldberg; Otto Simonsson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Individual differences shape the acute subjective psychedelic experience, but menstrual cycle status remains an understudied source of potential variability.
Methods: In a longitudinal observational study, 169 participants reported psychedelic use during the two-month study period. Participants were classified by menstrual cycle status during their most intense psychedelic experience: menstruating during the experience (n=15), menstruating but not during the experience (n=60), not menstruating (n=25), and male participants (n=69). Primary analyses examined associations between cycle status and ego dissolution (Ego Dissolution Inventory; EDI), mystical-type experience (Mystical Experience Questionnaire; MEQ), and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire; CEQ), adjusting for dose and age. Exploratory analyses examined MEQ and CEQ subscales and post-acute risk of harm to self and others.
Results: Participants menstruating during their experience reported higher EDI scores than both those menstruating but not during the experience and male participants (β=−0.89 and −0.68, ps≤.011). Cycle status was not associated with MEQ or CEQ scores. Exploratory analyses found higher physical distress and death subscale scores among participants menstruating during their experience than among those menstruating but not during the experience (β=−0.77 and −0.80, ps≤.005). Risk of post-acute harm to self and others was higher among those menstruating during the experience than among those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (OR=6.41, p=.022).
Conclusions: Menstrual cycle timing may be associated with aspects of the acute psychedelic experience, specifically ego dissolution and potentially risk of post-acute harm to self and others. These preliminary findings support further investigation of menstrual cycle status in psychedelic research.

articles_hidden.title: SaccadeJS: Webcam eye tracking for behavioral experiments in a web browser
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua R de Leeuw; Colin Mikulski; Alex Teabo; Cherrie Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Webcam eye tracking allows researchers to study eye movements in large, geographically diverse online samples, but its accuracy has limited it to coarse comparisons, such as which half or quadrant of the screen a participant is looking at. We introduce SaccadeJS, an open-source webcam eye tracker that runs entirely in the participant's browser. SaccadeJS uses a neural network to transform images of the eyes to features, which a ridge regression maps to screen positions. The network can be rapidly calibrated by computing new regression weights on a sample of fixations at known locations. To train the model, we collected a new dataset of 2,003 participants who fixated targets on their own laptop and desktop computers. In a validation study with 200 new online participants, the median participant's error was about 4% of the screen diagonal. That accuracy is enough to distinguish many more, and smaller, areas of interest than halves and quadrants. We also developed a timing calibration routine to measure each participant's camera lag. After correction, saccade latencies matched distributions from laboratory experiments. We report how different calibration strategies and image characteristics affect accuracy. SaccadeJS could be run in real time on about one third of the participants in the validation study; for others, the library processes frames in the background while the experiment runs. SaccadeJS can be used as standalone software for webcam eye tracking or in conjunction with jsPsych through a set of provided plugins for calibration, validation, and recording.

articles_hidden.title: The control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia
articles_hidden.authors: Georg Keller; Philipp Sterzer
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the last half century, we have made little progress in the treatment of schizophrenia. A key contributor to this is an insufficient understanding of what is causing the disorder. There are currently two broad families of hypotheses: those focused on a dopaminergic dysfunction, and those focused on a glutamatergic dysfunction. Based on recent findings that antipsychotic drugs exhibit cell-type specific and long-term effects on cortical circuit function, we integrate the two hypotheses into what we call the control limit hypothesis of schizophrenia. It builds on the assumption that schizophrenia is the result of a developmental miswiring of cortical circuits that is based on glutamatergic dysfunction and causes aberrant cortical activity dynamics. These cortical alterations likely underlie cognitive dysfunction, one of the core treatment-resistant symptoms of schizophrenia. The control limit hypothesis further postulates that the brain responds to and can partially mitigate these aberrant cortical dynamics by increasing dopamine levels in the striatum. When this regulatory system is driven to a control limit and dopamine levels exceed a given threshold, psychosis emerges. Beyond explaining much of the existing data, the hypothesis makes several predictions about cortical function testable in mice and humans.

articles_hidden.title: (Phon)aesthetics Beyond Sound: Sociocultural Associations, Aesthetic Appeal, and Perceived Valence in Sign Languages
articles_hidden.authors: Theresa Matzinger; Monika Boruta-Żywiczyńska
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aesthetic evaluations of languages depend not only on the linguistic signal but also on
language-external factors, notably familiarity with a language and the sociocultural
associations triggered by recognising it. For spoken languages, these factors are hard to
separate, because languages evoking strong cultural associations are usually also familiar. We
used sign languages to isolate the influence of sociocultural associations, testing hearing nonsigners
who were unfamiliar with American (ASL) and French (LSF) Sign Language but
familiar with the associated cultures. Participants rated 64 signs (32 ASL, 32 LSF; half
positively, half negatively valenced) for aesthetic appeal, perceived valence and, once given
the meaning, perceived iconicity. Half of participants were told which language each sign
belonged to, whereas the other half received no such information. Appeal ratings for ASL and
LSF differed only when the languages were indicated: the more participants liked French
relative to US-American culture, the more appealing they found LSF relative to ASL, and vice
versa. No such pattern emerged without this information. Sociocultural associations can thus
shape aesthetic evaluation of a language independently of direct linguistic experience.
Additionally, although participants did not know the signs’ meanings, positively valenced signs
were rated as more positive and, particularly in ASL, more appealing than negatively valenced
signs. This suggests that aesthetic and affective evaluations of signs are closely linked. Finally,
more iconic signs received valence ratings more closely aligned with their actual valence. To
our knowledge, this is the first extension of (phon)aesthetic research to sign languages.

articles_hidden.title: Neural responses to socioemotional information are more similar among siblings and relate to social competence
articles_hidden.authors: Sofia Scatolin; Elena Federici; Plamina Dimanova; Dennis Saikkonen; Jonathan Bugmann; Nora Maria Raschle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Socioemotional skills are fundamental to children’s well-being and development, yet the
neurodevelopmental processes through which familial relationships contribute to these skills
remain poorly understood. While socioemotional skills are partly heritable, they are also shaped by
social learning through interactions with others, including siblings. Sibling relationships represent
one of the earliest and most enduring social contexts throughout development and provide a
valuable context for investigating how familial relatedness is reflected in children's neural
processing of socioemotional information. However, little is known about whether siblings exhibit
similarities in these neural responses and how such similarities relate to socioemotional behavior.
In this study, we investigated whether sibling dyads show greater similarity in neural responses
during socioemotional processing than unrelated child dyads and whether such neural similarity is
associated with socioemotional functioning. To assess this, 120 children (6-14 years), including 39
sibling dyads, completed a naturalistic fMRI movie-watching task designed to elicit socioemotional
responses. Results showed that sibling dyads exhibited greater whole-brain functional neural
similarity during socioemotional processing than unrelated children across the whole brain. Region-
of-interest analyses further revealed greater functional neural similarity among siblings across
several prefrontal, temporal, and limbic regions, including the left ventromedial prefrontal cortex
(vmPFC). Moreover, greater similarity in left vmPFC responses, a region implicated in social
cognition, was associated with higher levels of socially competent behavior in both sibling and
unrelated dyads, suggesting that neural similarity may be particularly pronounced among children
with higher social competence. These findings highlight sibling relationships as an informative
context for investigating familial similarities in neural responses to socioemotional information and
their associations with socioemotional behavior during childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Not passive sponges: When attention wanes, our brains are less synchronized with the environment
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Greatti; Laura Batterink; Davide Crepaldi; Amy Finn
articles_hidden.abstract: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them. Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states? To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment—the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities—alongside fluctuations in attentional states. Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states. Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses. Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment. Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses. And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus. Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Musical Mood Regulation for Efficacy Beliefs and Hope in the Climate Crisis
articles_hidden.authors: Friederike Koehler; Dana Swarbrick; Suvi Saarikallio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Climate change is associated with a range of emotional responses, yet little is known about 
the role of music in regulating climate-related emotions and supporting adaptive 
psychological outcomes. Because music is widely used to regulate emotions and can foster 
positive affect, emotional coping, and resilience, it may also help individuals maintain hope 
when confronting the challenges of climate change. The present study examined whether 
music-based mood regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this 
relationship is mediated by climate efficacy beliefs. A cross-sectional online survey was 
completed by 310 adults. Participants reported their use of music to regulate climate-
related emotions, climate efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective 
efficacy, and collective outcome expectancy), and hope. Relationships among the variables 
were examined using correlation analyses and structural equation modeling. Several music-
based regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, 
were positively associated with hope. Some regulation strategies were also positively 
associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, 
whereas no significant bivariate associations emerged with collective efficacy. Structural 
equation modeling indicated a significant total indirect effect of music-based regulation on 
hope through climate efficacy beliefs. However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy 
emerged as significant mediators. Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy 
did not significantly mediate the association. The direct association between music-based 
regulation and hope remained significant, indicating partial mediation. These findings 
suggest that individuals who use music to regulate climate-related emotions report greater 
hope and that this association is partly explained by stronger perceptions of personal and 
collective capability. Climate efficacy beliefs emerged as a small yet significant pathway 
linking music-based regulation and hope. Music may therefore represent an accessible 
everyday resource that supports adaptive engagement with climate emotions and fosters 
hope in the context of climate change.

articles_hidden.title: Reading from childhood to adolescence: enduring influences of home environment on behaviour, motivation and proficiency
articles_hidden.authors: Sanne W van der Kleij; Jessie Ricketts; Laura Shapiro
articles_hidden.abstract: According to theoretical models of reading engagement, reading behaviours and reading motivation both influence reading proficiency. Additionally, annual surveys of young people’s reading engagement show decreasing numbers of children who report enjoying reading over time and across ages, but we lack longitudinal evidence confirming this decline. To examine the complex interaction between reading motivation, reading behaviour and reading proficiency, this study investigated: i) how young people’s motivation to read and reading behaviours change from age 10 to 15; ii) whether their engagement with reading is shaped by the home literacy environment (HLE); and iii) whether young people’s motivation to read determines their reading behaviours, in turn promoting reading comprehension. Data from a longitudinal study in [Blinded], UK (n = 598, 285 girls) were used to model the influence of HLE, reading motivation and reading behaviour on reading comprehension skills. Reading motivation, reading behaviour (i.e. time spent reading) and reading comprehension were assessed from age 10 to 15 and HLE was assessed in a subsample at age 11 (n = 299). Growth models showed that reading motivation and time spent reading declined from 11 to 13 years and then stabilised from age 14-15. However, trajectories of change differed across sex and socioeconomic status. In mediation models, the home literacy environment at age 11 was associated with children’s own reading engagement and showed direct and indirect associations with children’s reading comprehension outcomes. Our findings highlight the crucial influence of reading motivation on reading outcomes and uncover a longer-term role of HLE than previously assumed, extending well beyond childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Goals, Predictions, Valence: A Model Comparison of Agency Emergence
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas Richter; Marcel Raphael Schreiner
articles_hidden.abstract: The sense of agency (SoA), our feeling of control over actions and their environmental effects, has been explained through different theoretical models. This study compares three: the comparator model, proposing that SoA emerges from matching motor-based predictions to perceptual feedback, the ideomotor model, proposing that SoA emerges from monitoring goal achievement, and a self-serving bias model, proposing that SoA reflects self-attribution of positive and external attribution of negative outcomes. Participants performed a target-hitting task with manipulated visual feedback of positive or negative valence and rated their SoA on a subset of trials. The three models predict different SoA patterns based on motor activity appropriateness, goal achievement, and outcome valence. The ideomotor model best fit the empirical data, outperforming both alternatives, whereas evidence for an additional effect of outcome valence was ambiguous. These findings question the dominant role of motor-based predictions in SoA emergence and highlight goal achievement as a key determinant of SoA.

articles_hidden.title: Invariant agreement attraction effects: Distance and RC modification manipulations in Czech
articles_hidden.authors: Radim Lacina; Jakub Dotlacil
articles_hidden.abstract: Agreement attraction in comprehension often manifests itself as a speed-up in the of processing ungrammatical sentences where a verb carries the wrong number feature when a noun of the verb-matching number —the attractor—intervenes. The effect has been claimed to be insensitive to increased linear distance between the attractor and the agreement target. Recent studies on Czech found weak attraction effects attested only with case syncretic attractors. In two self-paced reading experiments with Czech comprehenders, we tested whether including material between the attractor and the verb could modulate attraction depending on whether the material was reinforcing the attractor's features or not. In Experiment 1, we aimed to increase attraction strength by modifying the attractor with a relative clause, giving it the subject feature and reinforcing its plurality. In Experiment 2, we matched the increased distance employed in Experiment 1 with feature-inert material to see if attraction was maintained. Our Bayes factor analysis provided us with evidence of a small attraction effect in the both experiments that did not differ meaningfully between the two. We therefore show that Czech exhibits online number attraction but of a tiny effect size. Our results further replicate earlier findings that distance does not affect agreement attraction in comprehension, as our effect sizes were comparable between the two experiments as well with previous work on Czech. Finally, they show that modifying attractors with relative clauses does not increase the strength of attraction speed-ups.

articles_hidden.title: On Bias in Detecting Bias: A Signal Detection Analysis of Attributions to Gender Discrimination
articles_hidden.authors: Marie Jakob; Anat Shechter; Jimmy Calanchini; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of Signal Detection Theory (SDT), with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers’ ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers’ judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical SDT analyses of attributions to
discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1 to 3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2 to 4) inform observers’ response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1 to 3), which reflects observers’ determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing.

articles_hidden.title: Designing Around the Human Creative Core: A Construct for Preserving Creative Agency in Human-AI Systems
articles_hidden.authors: Eran Barak-Medina
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative AI can increasingly perform the parts of professional work where a person's judgment and sense of identity are most engaged. The common design instinct is to automate wherever AI can plausibly take over, treating capability as the test. This efficiency-first instinct can erode the skill, judgment, ownership, and professional identity. Human-Centered AI frameworks show how to structure collaboration and keep people in control, but not which elements of a given workflow sustain a person's creative agency. This paper introduces the Human Creative Core: the subset of workflow elements where a person's cognitive contribution and psychological investment converge, identified through four dimensions, strategic intention, signature judgment, identity and ownership, and developmental function. The construct yields a design principle, complement the core and automate the periphery, and a method for locating the core in a given workflow. The method was taught and applied in a graduate instructional design course, and is demonstrated here across five professional cases. The contribution is a design construct and a repeatable method for building AI that preserves, and can strengthen, a person's creative agency rather than dissolving it.

articles_hidden.title: A Bi-Factor Generalized Cognitive Diagnosis Model Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Rodrigo Schames Kreitchmann; Pablo Nájera; Francisco José Abad
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) are often applied to constructs that are largely unidimensional in nature (e.g., mathematics, reading, mental health status) where a set of discrete attributes coexists with a dominant general proficiency dimension. This article presents the bi-factor CDM model (BF-CDM), which partitions item responses into a direct effect of continuous general proficiency and a discrete attribute-mastery tier, allowing mastery classifications to be made beyond what is attributable to general ability. By modeling both tiers explicitly, the BF-CDM makes it possible to evaluate the contribution of the discrete tier itself. Specifically, it can show whether the hypothesized attributes carry diagnostic information beyond general proficiency, both through model comparison with the nested unidimensional model and through the reliability of the attribute-specific component. A simulation study manipulating sample size, test length, number of attributes, and attribute-tier discrimination shows accurate recovery of item and person parameters, and of the model-implied response functions. An application to reading comprehension data from PISA illustrates the practical value of the model: reliability of attribute-mastery classifications drops substantially once variance attributable to general proficiency is partialled out, indicating that much of the apparent diagnostic precision obtained under a saturated attribute structure reflects a single dominant general factor.

articles_hidden.title: Psychology’s Missing Matter
articles_hidden.authors: Oulmann Zerhouni
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology's replication and generalizability shortcomings suggest that, although valuable, statistical and incentive reforms have not stabilized core constructs. I argue that residual implicit dualism, characterized by the acceptance of loosely defined constructs supported by metaphors and weakly connected to biologically specific mechanisms, contributes to this instability. I propose the Materialist Model of Psychological Science (MMPS): a pluralism-friendly framework based on four axioms (physical realization, multi-level constraint, evolutionary plausibility and mechanistic falsifiability). These axioms are operationalized via an eight-criterion ontological audit with phase-based governance (from prototype to maturity). When applied to three illustrative cases: ego depletion, implicit bias, and fear conditioning. The audit reveals a systematic link between mechanistic density (material anchoring, perturbation-sensitive predictions, and cross-context invariance) and replication robustness. The paper outlines complementary reforms, such as mechanism-focused preregistration, invariance profiling in multilab work, perturbation toolkits and open construct registries, that redirect theory building towards cumulative, vertically integrated knowledge, while safeguarding exploratory diversity through graded evidential expectations. The MMPS adds explicit mechanistic, evolutionary, and perturbational constraints to classical construct validity. The result is a practical foundation that converts diffuse calls for 'better theory' into concrete, auditable criteria for accepting, revising or suspending psychological construct

articles_hidden.title: Does Teacher Praise Make Children Feel Less Smart? Two Preregistered Virtual Reality Experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Lena-Emilia Schenker; Jellie Sierksma; Milica Nikolic; Eddie Brummelman
articles_hidden.abstract: Does teacher praise make children feel less smart? When two students perform equally, teachers might praise the student they believe worked harder, implicitly conveying to that student that they have lower ability. We tested this hypothesis through two preregistered experiments in a novel Virtual Reality classroom with children aged 7-13 (Study 1: N = 212, Study 2: N = 225). After the child and a virtual classmate performed equally on a task, the teacher praised the child, the classmate, both, or neither. Contrary to hypotheses, there was no evidence that praise made children feel less smart, think that the teacher believed they were less smart, or experience elevated physiological arousal (heart rate, heart rate variability, blushing, skin conductance). Study 2 suggests that children instead viewed praise as a sign of being liked by the teacher. Our studies offer robust evidence that teacher praise may not make children feel less smart.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of cash-out availability on online betting behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Barnabas Szaszi; Wei Yue Hung; Peter Szecsi; Pál Kolumbán; Márton Kolozsvári; Miklos Bognar; Arife Yesilöz; Mark Griffiths; Zsolt Demetrovics
articles_hidden.abstract: The rise of online sports betting, facilitated by technological innovations such as the cash-out feature, has transformed the gambling landscape. While cash-outs have been suggested to intensify problematic gambling behaviors, empirical studies to date have been correlational, leaving a gap in determining causal evidence. In the present Registered Report, the proposed study will investigate the direct impact of the perceived availability of the cash-out feature on various facets of gambling behavior in an online experiment. Hungarian residents with online gambling history will be informed that they will have the chance to gamble with real money on sports events. Following random allocation, half of the participants will be told that they will have the option to cash out their bets before the outcome of the sports event is known, while the other half will not. The study will compare the proportion of participants placing bets, bet sizes, and bet risks between the two groups. Furthermore, the study will explore the differential effects of the cash-out feature on specific high-risk subgroups. The findings are likely to have significant implications for the design of online betting platforms, contribute to regulatory frameworks, and inform the design of interventions aimed at minimizing gambling-related harm.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Participation, Towards Meaningful Inclusion:  An Experience-Sensitive Approach to Inquiry with Children and Young People with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND)
articles_hidden.authors: Georgia Pavlopoulou; Elaine McGreevy; Vasileios Sideropoulos
articles_hidden.abstract: Contemporary participatory research has focused predominantly on procedural consultation while paying comparatively little attention to how participation is experienced by children and young people (CYP) and research teams, and how those experiences shape knowledge production. We argue that lived experience continues to occupy a peripheral position within scientific knowledge production, often informing rather than constituting evidence. To address this limitation, we propose the Experience-Sensitive Method of Inquiry (ESMI), a methodological orientation that places lived experience at the centre of knowledge production. ESMI is grounded in eight interconnected experience-sensitive dimensions that together provide its epistemological foundation. Central to this framework is participatory reflexivity, conceptualised as an ongoing methodological practice through which researchers examine how relationships, assumptions, environments and methodological choices shape what becomes knowable. Participatory reflexivity therefore functions as the mechanism through which experiential knowledge is recognised, interpreted, and integrated throughout the research process. In practice, ESMI may be operationalised through three interconnected methodological principles: Agency, Belonging and Collaboration (ABC). These principles function as a practical reflexive heuristic for designing, conducting, interpreting and translating participatory research. ESMI shifts attention from whether participation occurs to how participation is experienced and how experiential knowledge influences evidence generation. Although developed in the context of research with CYP with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities, ESMI is intended as a transdisciplinary methodological orientation for experience-informed inquiry. It has two interconnected aims: first, to improve how children and young people with SEND experience research; and second, to strengthen the relevance, interpretability and trustworthiness of the evidence produced. The framework may inform a wide range of methodologies, including trials, longitudinal cohort studies, Delphi studies, experimental research, and qualitative inquiry, from question formulation through to dissemination. The extent to which these proposed benefits are realised remains an empirical question requiring future evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable Effects of Sleep and Memory Suppression on Emotional Memory Processing
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Klets; Marcus Harrington; Aidan J Horner; Scott Cairney
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to retrieve memories of adverse events without fully reinstating their associated emotional charge is a hallmark of an adaptive memory system. This decoupling of emotional reactivity from episodic memory has been linked to two key processes: memory suppression during wakefulness and memory consolidation during sleep. Yet, the combined influences of wakeful suppression and sleep-associated memory processing on emotional affect during retrieval are unknown. We sought to address this gap in the current study. Participants learned to associate images of faces with emotionally negative and neutral scenes and then either suppressed or retrieved the scenes when presented with the faces as reminder cues. They then took a nap monitored with polysomnography (nap group) or remained awake for an equivalent period of time in the laboratory (wake group). Before and after the delay, emotional responses to the negative and neutral scenes were evaluated using self-report, skin conductance responses (SCRs) and heart rate deceleration (HRD) to index changes in emotional affect that were attributable to memory suppression and/or sleep-associated consolidation. Memory suppression had no impact on self-reported emotion, SCRs or HRD in either the nap or wake group. However, subjective emotional responses decreased significantly more after sleep than wake. These findings support a role for sleep-associated consolidation in reducing the affective salience of emotional memories.

articles_hidden.title: Shared Cause Adjusted Mediation (SCAM): Introduction of method with empirical applications
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: A genuine mediated effect, also called an indirect effect, is the part of the relationship between a predictor (X) and an outcome (Y) that operates through a third variable, called a mediator (M). However, estimated mediated effects do not prove genuine mediation as they only require variables to be correlated and correlations may be due to confounding. Here, I propose adjusting for effects that are expected if the predictor, outcome, and mediator(s) share a common latent cause. In an application of this method on four studies using serial mediation analyses, only 5 of 24 (21%) reported effects remained statistically significant after such adjustment for a shared latent cause.

articles_hidden.title: Pre-registered protocol: Felt Intelligence reads scored by the person. Hypotheses H4 to H7, count C1, frozen lexicon and scoring rules. No results reported.
articles_hidden.authors: Abhishek kumar Raysingh
articles_hidden.abstract: This is a pre-registration, not a result. It records, before any scoring, the tests a small research project will run on Felt Intelligence (FI), a reading of a person that the person scores: a dated line about their own past is spoken, they answer "That's me" or "Not quite", and their answer outranks the reading. Four hypothesis tests (H4, H5, H6, H7) and one descriptive count (C1) are stated with their populations, windows, measures, pass rules, readability thresholds and fail actions. H4 to H6 were first published on satya.org on 17 and 18 October 2026 with SHA-256 fingerprints; H7 and C1 were written on 5 November 2026. The identical text was registered on the Open Science Framework on 5 November 2026 at 10:41 UTC (osf.io/krs8a). H7 is unrun; its window opens only when the shuffled-delivery build is live, and that date will be published before any tap counts. The window label on the first-reflection count (529) is being settled and logged before a single claim is scored. No outcome is promised. Nothing here is called proven. Reads are published pass, fail, not yet decisive, or "not enough people yet", with denominators, at satya.org/research.

articles_hidden.title: Testing implications of the network theory of mental disorders in intensive short-term treatment
articles_hidden.authors: Sabrina Benz; Lea Schumacher; Samy Egli; Johannes Kopf-Beck
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance. Network theory is increasingly used to inform targeted and personalized treatment by identifying symptoms and interactions that maintain psychopathology. Yet, its prediction that successful treatment should weaken symptom interactions remains insufficiently tested.
Objective. To examine whether temporal interactions among depression and anxiety symptoms and global network connectivity decrease during short, intensive inpatient/day-clinic treatment, as predicted by network theory.
Design. Preregistered secondary analysis of OPTIMA, a randomized controlled trial conducted September 2017 to October 2020; analyses were conducted January 2025 to May 2026.
Setting. Single-center inpatient and day-clinic treatment in Germany with weekly symptom assessments.
Participants. Adults aged 18 to 75 years with moderate to severe depression without psychotic symptoms. Of 1370 patients assessed, 292 were randomized, and 288 were included in this analysis.
Interventions. Seven weeks of schema therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, or individual supportive therapy, with up to 2 individual and 2 group sessions weekly plus clinically indicated pharmacotherapy and concomitant care.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Changes in temporal interactions among 6 core depression and anxiety symptoms and in global network connectivity, estimated using a time-varying longitudinal network model. Exploratory stability landscapes characterized changes in network-implied symptom states.
Results. Among 288 participants (mean [SD] age, 43.6 [13.6] years; 55.6% female), only 3 of 36 temporal symptom associations changed substantially, although symptom severity decreased. Mean absolute network strength did not substantially decrease from 0.55 (95% CI, 0.47-0.64) at treatment start to 0.46 (95% CI, 0.38-0.54) after 7 weeks. Still, the network model could explain symptom trajectories well (Bayesian pseudo-R² ranging from 0.43 to 0.54) and exploratory network-implied stability landscapes indicated a system shift toward lower-symptom states.
Conclusions and Relevance. These findings provide limited support for the prediction that successful treatment reduces global connectivity in short, intensive treatment settings. In such settings, treatment-related change in symptom severity may be reflected in a reduction in general likelihood of symptom occurrence, but not necessarily in changes in symptom interactions, raising questions about long-term vulnerability. On the other hand, global symptom connectivity alone may not sufficiently characterize a healthy symptom system, and the role of specific symptom interactions warrants further investigation.
Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03287362.

articles_hidden.title: Inequality Can Increase Stealing, Reduce Trust, and Undermine Cooperation, Even When It Is Invisible
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Buzan; Daniel Nettle
articles_hidden.abstract: Higher inequality is associated with higher crime, lower trust, and lower cooperation, but the mechanisms producing these associations remain unclear. Inequality produces compositional effects through changing individuals’ resource levels, regardless of whether or not it is perceived. Inequality’s visibility may have further effects precisely because people perceive it. In Study 1 (N = 496; 64 groups), participants played a multiplayer experimental game in groups of eight, choosing to steal from one another, cooperate, or work alone. Participants’ were never informed of others' points levels. Inequality in the initial points distribution increased stealing rates, lowered trust, and reduced the rate of cooperation, but only when there was a points threshold below which it was disastrous to fall. Study 2 (N = 1,014; 132 groups) replicated these findings. It also tested the additional role of visibility by varying whether participants had no information about others’ points, knew their partner’s points, or knew the group’s point distribution. Making inequality visible had no meaningful effect on any outcome. Together, these findings provide evidence for compositional, but not visibility, effects of inequality: distributing resources unequally around a threshold increased crime, reduced trust, and lowered cooperation, whether or not inequality was visible.

articles_hidden.title: Exploration for gains and loss-avoidance across the human lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Waltmann; Caroline Emily Phelps; Lorenz Deserno; Siyu Wang; Ben Eppinger; Robert C Wilson; Andrea M.F. Reiter
articles_hidden.abstract: Navigating an uncertain world, we constantly face the explore-exploit dilemma: should we stick with what we know, or explore options that may or may not prove better? An influential theory proposes that humans solve this dilemma through a division of labor in time: explore in childhood, exploit in old age. Our work adds critical empirical nuance to this theory. Exploration can manifest as deliberate information-seeking (“directed exploration”) or choice randomness (“random exploration”), and these strategies are employed differently for gain-seeking and loss-avoidance. Here, we ask how these modes of exploration relate to one another and jointly shape decision-making across the lifespan. A cross-sectional sample of 254 participants aged 8–79 performed a bandit task dissociating directed and random exploration in gain-seeking and loss-avoidance contexts. Factor analysis revealed three factors driving behavior: two domain-specific factors reflecting information-seeking for gains and loss-avoidance, respectively, and a domain-general factor reflecting choice randomness. Directed exploration for gains increased steadily and well into young adulthood before declining in older adulthood, whereas directed exploration for loss-avoidance changed little across the lifespan. Children and older adults, relative to young adults, were characterized by greater choice randomness across contexts, even when exploration was disadvantageous. Though working memory and processing speed accounted for some of these effects, independent effects of age remained. Our findings demonstrate that exploration is not a unitary phenomenon: it encompasses dissociable subprocesses – some domain-specific and others domain-general – with distinct developmental timelines that are shaped by cognitive maturation and decline as well as factors beyond cognitive ability.

articles_hidden.title: Perception of occluded motion depends on post-occlusion motion information
articles_hidden.authors: Lina Teichmann; Grace Edwards; Austin Kyle Behel; Chris Ian Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: Moving objects frequently become occluded from view, yet we often experience a compelling sense of their continued motion and position during occlusion. Despite this subjective impression, recent behavioral and neuroimaging evidence suggests that representations of moving objects during occlusion may be limited. Here, across four experiments, we investigated 1) the accuracy of object localization during dynamic occlusion, 2) the motion information which may support successful position judgments, and 3) the relationship between gaze behavior and localization performance. In Experiment 1a, participants estimated the position of a moving object at unpredictable time points during occlusion. Position estimates were highly inaccurate, with errors increasing as objects travelled further behind the occluder. Increasing object speed exacerbated these errors in Experiment 1b, whereas decreasing speed improved performance. With decreased speed, there was also an increase in pre-occlusion motion information, which may aid object localization during dynamic occlusion. In Experiment 2, we found post-occlusion motion information could support accurate judgments of object reappearance. The necessity of post-occlusion information was further supported in Experiment 3, when removing post-occlusion motion information while testing a predictable intercept location resulted in inaccurate estimations. Across experiments, gaze position predicted behavioral errors, with eye movement strategies varying according to task demands. Together, these findings suggest that the position of moving objects is poorly represented during dynamic occlusion, despite our compelling subjective experience of their occluded location. Instead, accurate judgments depend critically on information acquired after the object re-emerges, consistent with a postdictive reconstruction of occluded object position.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological Acceptance Across Adulthood: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Lital Levit-Frank; Dikla Segel-Karpas; Nir Shalev
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological acceptance is an emotion regulation strategy in which people allow thoughts and feelings to arise and pass without trying to change them. Although theory implies that acceptance will increase with age, empirical evidence remains fragmented, with studies varying in sample characteristics, effect sizes, and age ranges. To address this gap and clarify the association between age and psychological acceptance we conducted a meta-analysis. Our preregistered search (PROSPERO CRD420251103979) identified 25 studies with 31 independent samples (N = 12,561). Random-effects pooling yielded a small but robust positive association between age and psychological acceptance (r = 0.077, 95% CI 0.027–0.127), despite substantial heterogeneity between studies. Specifically, studies that sampled wider age ranges reported stronger associations, so narrow age spans may understate the association.

articles_hidden.title: From Lab to App (and Back): A Conceptual Framework for Evidence-Based Digital Mental Health Interventions in Children and Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Solvejg Kassandra Kleber; Philipp Axel Raßbach; Hans-Henrik Dassow; Joschka Haltaufderheide; Elisabeth Höhne; Michael Kölch; André Markus; Nora Mierzwa; Robert Ranisch; Michael A Rapp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental health problems represent a major global challenge, with access to appropriate care for children and adolescents remaining severely limited. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) can offer scalable, accessible support beyond traditional clinical settings. Despite a constantly growing number of youths DMHIs, the evidence base is constrained, due to a lack of replication and follow-up studies, scarce side-effect examination, and heterogeneous designs and characteristics. This is particularly concerning regarding young people as a vulnerable population. Knowledge of intervention processes is important to advance the field of DMHIs, while this topic is under researched in both DMHIs and traditional interventions for youth. Reaching full potential of DMHIs for youth requires an integrated research and development approach.

We consulted experts from multiple disciplines, including youths psychiatrists, psychologists, psychotherapists, computer scientists and ethicists specializing in digital mental health, to integrate the current state of knowledge into a conceptual framework.

The conceptual framework “From Lab to App (and Back)” emphasizes continuous exchange between DMHI research and development, with participatory collaboration, embedded ethics, and science communication relevant in all stages. We outline that DMHIs are particularly well suited to generate insight into mechanisms of change and discuss key factors in DMHIs for youth. Furthermore, we address the need for more unified conceptualizations and standardized reporting and illustrate a working intervention process model for youths DMHIs to induce an overarching research agenda.
Overall, the framework provides a structured pathway toward scientifically rigorous and clinically meaningful digital innovation in youth mental health research and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Endogenous Attention Effects on Metacognitive Awareness: A Proof-of-Concept DLPFC-cTBS Study
articles_hidden.authors: Antonio Martin; Tzu-Yu Hsu; Joaquim Streicher
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: While endogenous attention is known to influence visual metacognition, it remains unclear whether these effects occur without altering perceptual performance, and what specific role the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) plays in mediating them.
Objective: We investigated whether spatial attention modulates subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency independently of perceptual sensitivity (d′), and whether the
DLPFC contributes to these effects.
Methods: Across two experiments, participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice discrimination task embedded within a Posner cueing paradigm, utilizing adaptive
staircases. We assessed reaction times, signal detection metrics, subjective visibility ratings, and metacognitive efficiency. In Experiment 2, this task was performed following
continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) targeting either the bilateral DLPFC or an active control site (primary somatosensory cortex, S1).
Results: In Experiment 1, invalid cues prolonged reaction times, shifted response bias, and impaired metacognitive efficiency, without affecting overall accuracy, subjective
visibility, or perceptual sensitivity. In Experiment 2, whereas these attentional effects persisted following control S1-cTBS, they were significantly disrupted following DLPFC-cTBS, despite objective perceptual performance remaining stable. Furthermore, trial-by- trial analyses indicated that DLPFC disruption impairs adaptive metacognitive updating.
Conclusions: Endogenous spatial attention modulates visual metacognitive efficiency independently of objective perceptual sensitivity. Notably, our neuromodulatory findings suggest that the DLPFC does not generate metacognitive contents directly, but rather regulates the executive and attentional processes that inform metacognitive evaluations.

articles_hidden.title: Do Executive Function Interventions Improve Children's Everyday Executive Functioning? A Systematic Review and Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Behavioral Report Measures
articles_hidden.authors: Mayara Azevedo; Pedro Fernandes Bernardino; Anelisa dos Anjos Queiroz; André Luiz Monteiro Trindade; Rachel Foster; Paulo Guirro Laurence
articles_hidden.abstract: Executive function (EF) interventions are widely used to promote children's cognitive and behavioral development. However, previous meta-analyses on EF intervention outcomes have relied exclusively on laboratory-based performance tasks, leaving unclear whether intervention effects generalize to children's everyday functioning. The present systematic review and three-level meta-analysis synthesized evidence from studies using behavioral report measures of EF, including questionnaires and rating scales completed by parents, teachers, children, or researchers. Seven electronic databases were systematically searched following PRISMA guidelines. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria, contributing 83 effect sizes from 2,142 typically developing children. A three-level random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to account for the dependency among multiple outcomes reported within studies. Overall, EF interventions produced a small but statistically significant improvement in everyday executive functioning (g = 0.17, 95% CI [0.03, 0.32]). Moderator analyses suggested larger effects for EF-specific curricula than for other intervention approaches, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of studies within intervention categories. The review also revealed important gaps in the literature: behavioral report outcomes remain substantially underrepresented relative to laboratory measures, nearly 80% of studies relied on the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF), and almost half of the evidence originated from the United States. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence that EF interventions can produce modest improvements in children's everyday executive functioning while highlighting the need for more diverse behavioral measures, greater replication of intervention programs, and increased attention to ecologically valid outcomes when evaluating intervention effectiveness.

articles_hidden.title: Child and parent mental health symptoms in Nigeria: A genetically informed study of pre-school twins in a Low-/Middle-Income Country
articles_hidden.authors: Olakunle Oginni; Oluwatosin Olorunmoteni; Olusola Jeje; Olatokunbo Oguns; Kehinde Ayodele; Abimbola Onigbinde; Boladale Mapayi; Fruhling Rijsdijk; Anita Thapar; Frances Rice
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Ninety percent of the world’s children live in Low-/Middle-Income Countries (LMICs),
but relatively little is known about children’s mental health risk in these settings. Using a
genetically informative twin-family design, we estimated parent-child associations for mental
health symptoms (MHSs), indirect effects through specific risk/protective factors, and how
parental MHSs impact genetic/environmental influences on child MHSs in Nigeria.

Methods
We recruited 320 twin pairs (aged 3-5 years) and both parents in two Nigerian towns.
Participants were assessed for MHSs (emotional/behavioural symptoms in children; anxiety,
depressive and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder symptoms in parents), and selected
risk/protective factors (adverse home environments, adverse childhood experiences, poor
physical health; and religiosity, parental warmth and prosociality). We used structural equation
modelling to test parent-child MHS associations, and mediation by risk/protective factors. We
estimated latent genetic (A), shared environmental (C) and individual-specific environmental
(E) influences on child MHSs, and how parent MHSs impact these influences using univariate
twin models.

Results
Child MHSs were significantly associated with MHSs in both parents. The strongest
indirect effects for parent-child MHS associations were through adverse childhood experiences
and diminished parental warmth. Others indirect pathways involved poor physical health and
diminished prosociality. Latent A and C influences each explained 22-29% of the individual
differences in children’s MHSs. Independent of A influences, C influences were impacted by
parents’ MHSs.

Conclusion
Our findings indicate that potentially modifiable environmental pathways are important
for understanding parent-child MHS associations for very young children in a LMIC, and these
may inform intervention design. Larger and more rigorous genetically informative designs are
needed to replicate and extend our findings.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Sleep and the Daytime Course of Anhedonia in Adolescent Depression: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah E. Marshall; Linda Nduka; Tahjanee Givens; Caroline M. Miller; Mollie Davis; Chana Engel; Kenneth Towbin; Daniel Pine; Katharina Kircanski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mounting evidence suggests that sleep disturbances and depression are linked through disruptions in reward processing. This pathway may be especially relevant to adolescent depression, as adolescence is characterized by more frequent sleep disturbances, reduced sleep, and refinement of reward circuitry.
Aim: This preregistered study uses high-density ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from the Characterization and Treatment of Adolescent Depression Studies (CTADS) cohort (collected from 2023 to 2026) to test sleep disturbances and duration as predictors of anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia and to determine whether effects exhibit diurnal variation.
Methods: Sixty-five adolescents (12-18 years; 43 female, 22 male; 41 with major depressive disorder, 24 healthy volunteers) completed 120 EMA prompts over 30 days. Participants reported prior-night sleep disturbances and duration once per day, and anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia four times per day. We ran two Bayesian multilevel linear models, estimating anticipatory and consummatory anhedonia, respectively, as functions of prior-night sleep disturbances, time of day, diagnostic group, and their interactions. We then ran two exploratory models assessing sleep duration in the same manner.
Results: In adolescents with MDD, whereas self-reported sleep disturbances did not predict anhedonia, longer sleep duration predicted both lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia. In healthy adolescents, greater sleep disturbances predicted lower anticipatory and lower consummatory anhedonia. Effects of sleep disturbances on anhedonia tended to increase across the day in adolescents with MDD and healthy adolescents.
Conclusions: Sleep disturbances and duration differentially predict next-day anhedonia in adolescents with MDD. For adolescent MDD patients, treatments that target sleep duration, as opposed to sleep disturbances, could provide more immediate effects on anhedonia. Time-of-day moderation effects suggest the mechanisms through which sleep disturbances (but not sleep duration) affect anhedonia may involve diurnal biological processes.

articles_hidden.title: Data-informed online teacher training to improve student engagement during the transition to high school: a cluster randomised trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Noetel; Theresa Dicke; Philip David Parker; Nikos Ntoumanis; Mark R. Beauchamp; Alexander Yeung; Ryan Hulteen; Diego Vasconcellos; Asghar Ahmadi; Jiesi Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: Teacher-focused interventions typically select targets from a single motivational theory using researcher judgement. We tested whether data-informed target selection could improve student engagement during the transition to secondary school. Using elastic net regression on two-wave data from 1,799 students, we screened 71 teacher behaviours from four theories and identified the six (per subject) that best predicted engagement in physical education (PE) and mathematics.
